news.title: Lone juror’s holdout in the Lindsay Clancy trial is a true act of courage
news.text:
‘He couldn’t get over the fact that Clancy viciously killed her children.”

Those are the words of one of the insufferably condescending female jurors from the Lindsay Clancy mistrial who have gone public with their disdain for the lone male juror who refused to go along with their not guilty verdict.

Good for him.

The children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, have been the forgotten victims in this case.

The Massachusetts nurse does not dispute that she strangled her children one by one on Jan. 24, 2023, with exercise bands around their necks after she sent her husband, Patrick, out on an errand.

Patrick returned to his kids dead and his wife bleeding on the snow-covered yard after she cut her wrists and throat and leaped out a bedroom window 12 feet above the ground, rendering herself paralyzed from the waist down. Rather than accepting blame, Lindsay, 36, pleaded not guilty, claiming she could not tell right from wrong at the time because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, even though evidence for that was thin.

Withstood pressure

A mistrial was called last Friday because the jury of nine women and three men could not agree on a verdict after more than seven days of deliberations so contentious that yelling reportedly could be heard outside the room.

Now that several of the jurors have come out and exposed themselves, we can see the immense pressure that the lone holdout juror was under day after day in that jury room, being harangued and browbeaten by women infuriated that he refused to be persuaded by their self-proclaimed superior wisdom.

Jury forewoman Roni Carlson, a former elementary school teacher, Kellie Farina, a chef for a senior center, and Paula Devlin, who does work for a defense contractor, were interviewed on camera by NBC10 Boston, and it’s hard to imagine a more smug group lacking in self-awareness or any humility. They revealed that there were a number of nurses and teachers on the jury.

“He was very arrogant,” Devlin said of the holdout. “He did not take anything that anybody said.”

She complained there were multiple nurses on the jury who took it on themselves to explain the toxicology reports to the holdout juror.

“He tried to ask a question about the medications,” said Devlin. “We had the toxicology report. We could see exactly the amounts. The nurses in the room spoke to that. And talked to that.

“And they spoke to that . . . And he just completely disregarded the information that they gave him.” As was his right.

Carlson, the forewoman, said she thought they’d won the argument at one point. “He admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited . . . And then he said, ‘But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity.’ ”

As was his right.

Another woman, Juror No. 5, spoke to CBS Boston anonymously in defense of the holdout:

“The majority of people . . . was very firm in their stance and their beliefs from the beginning . . . The standalone juror was not the only one who refused to see things from the other side so I’m going to defend [him]. There were some big personalities in that room.”

Originally, she thought Lindsay” was guilty and she was criminally responsible for it, and maybe I still believe that in a certain way.” Several other jurors reportedly felt the same way but over time were persuaded to find Lindsay not guilty — all but the holdout.

Lawyer’s big show

The outspoken female jurors absolutely loved Lindsay’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, and gushed about how “entertaining” and “compassionate” he was. In their minds he had proved that Lindsay was not a bad mother and she “loved her children” and that was all that mattered.

Yet Reddington behaved like an emotional bully, inside and outside the court, especially when he put a target on the holdout juror, whom he blamed for the mistrial in an extended public tantrum outside the court on Friday.

“I hope that guy can sleep well at night,” Reddington said. In court he called the same juror a “liar” and said he “stole seven weeks of the life” of the other jurors,” which is rich considering that in the entire seven-week trial Reddington barely mentioned the three entire lives stolen from the Clancy children by his client.

Reddington also fueled false internet rumors that Patrick was involved in the killing of his own children by refusing to exonerate him when asked and instead praising the TikTok sleuths who have damned Patrick.

“I certainly don’t dismiss them. It’s amazing what people on TikTok . . . how they’re able to ferret out facts and they do investigations.”

Reddington must have realized he went too far because this week he appeared on “CBS Mornings” and recanted, saying, “It’s obvious that Patrick was a man who stood by his wife through all of the difficulty. [He] ought to be able to move on with his life.”

Despite Reddington’s flaws, the outspoken female jurors preferred him to prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, whom they criticized as lacking “compassion” and being “unprofessional.”

For the children

The prosecutors were entirely professional. Did Carlson and pals disdain them because of their plump appearance, because they don’t have time to go to Pilates every morning?

Sprague and Buckingham have 50 years of prosecutorial experience between them and children of their own, earning modest salaries for draining work in child protection cases. They did their best, although their speedy four-day jury selection leaves something to be desired.

Their boss, District Attorney Tim Cruz, who has been protecting the 500,000 residents of Plymouth County for the past 25 years, was heckled relentlessly outside the court Friday.

The son of a plumber with children and grandchildren of his own, he is the longest serving DA in Massachusetts, even though he is a Republican in a Democrat-majority area.

Plymouth has street signs declaring it “America’s Hometown,” since it is where the Pilgrims arrived on the Mayflower in 1620 and founded the first permanent European settlement in New England. The affluent, predominantly white town, which voted for Kamala Harris over Donald Trump by almost 10 points in 2024, also adopted the slogan “No Place for Hate.”

Officials abandoned that name last year, but it still appears on some signs around town.

In spite of the heckling, Cruz spoke with understated dignity, saying: “I understand that this has been an emotional trial for everybody . . . But in the end I bring it all back to the child victims in this case, Cora, Dawson, and Callan . . .

“Children were murdered, and it’s our job to seek justice.”

Justice is important, regardless of feelings. The trial was not just about Lindsay and her tragedy. It was about the children and precedents set for child murder. Already there are reports of at least one copycat murder.

For the sake of all the other children yet to be born, we cannot afford to become a society that normalizes mothers killing their babies.
news.summary: The children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, have been the forgotten victims in this case.

news.title: Nearly Half of Voters Think Supreme Court is Biased for Trump: Poll
news.text: Nearly half of registered voters believe the Supreme Court is biased in favor of President Donald Trump, according to a new Economist/YouGov poll, as Trump has increasingly sought the justices' intervention on election-related matters ahead of the midterms. The poll, conducted September 4-8 among 1,469 registered voters, found that 44 percent said the Supreme Court is biased in favor of Trump, while just 12 percent said it is biased against him. Another 27 percent said the Court is not biased and treats Trump fairly, while 18 percent were unsure. The poll's margin of error is 3.4 percent. The perception is sharply divided along partisan lines. Eighty-one percent of voters who supported then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election said the Court is biased in Trump's favor, compared with just 9 percent of Trump voters. Among Democrats, 77 percent said the Court favors Trump, while 20 percent of Republicans said it is biased against him and nearly 50 percent said it treats him fairly. The survey shows that 44 percent of independents said the Court favors Trump, 23 percent said it treats him fairly and 8 percent said it is biased against him. Newsweek reached out to the Supreme Court via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know The latest survey also found that the Supreme Court's overall standing has weakened since earlier this summer. Fifty-six percent of registered voters said they disapprove of how the Court is handling its job, compared with 34 percent who approve. In an Economist/YouGov poll conducted in July, 50 percent disapproved and 36 percent approved. At the same time, the share of respondents describing the Court as conservative rose from 44 percent in July to 49 percent in the latest survey, while the share calling it liberal increased only slightly, from 9 percent to 10 percent. The timing comes as the Supreme Court faced a growing number of politically consequential election disputes ahead of the November midterms. The Court recently declined to reinstate a Republican-backed congressional map in Missouri, while it has also issued other rulings affecting the Trump administration and Republican campaign efforts. With registered voters seemingly divided over the Court's ideological direction and its relationship with Trump, any future ruling could further shape public perceptions of the judiciary. The new poll also shows that 47 percent think the Supreme Court's recent rulings have given Trump too much power. Thirty percent said the rulings give him about the right amount of power, 8 percent said too little power, and 15 percent are not sure. Seventy-three percent said the president should always obey orders from the Court, even if he believes they are wrong. Eleven percent said no and 16 percent said not sure. A randomly assigned half of the respondents were asked that question, the poll notes. A July Economist/YouGov poll found mixed views of individual Supreme Court justices. Amy Coney Barrett was viewed favorably by 23 percent of respondents and unfavorably by 38 percent, while 29 percent viewed Clarence Thomas favorably and 41 percent unfavorably. Chief Justice John Roberts had a 25 percent favorable rating and 36 percent unfavorable rating, while Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was viewed favorably by 34 percent and unfavorably by 26 percent. The poll found that the net favorability ratings of Justices Thomas, Barrett and Kavanaugh all soured compared to a similar poll conducted a year earlier, reflecting a shift in Americans' opinions of the Court. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The survey comes as Trump has increasingly sought the justices' intervention on election-related matters ahead of the midterms.

news.title: Gavin Newsom expresses 'openness' to packing SCOTUS, calls Electoral College system 'perverted'
news.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed "openness" to reforming the Supreme Court and claimed the Electoral College "perverted" politics during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon on his podcast Tuesday. Near the end of the interview, Lemon directly asked Newsom, a rumored 2028 candidate, whether he believed the judicial branch needed to be expanded, an idea pushed by several Democratic figures, including former Vice President Kamala Harris. "My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded," Newsom said. "And I was making a case for the ethical reforms and term limits, 18 years, which I was making a case a year ago. I'm more open to it on the basis of those district court arguments, which are not terrible arguments." DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION "Is that a yes?" Lemon asked. "I'm finding myself evolving on it. I normally have very clear conviction on things. I've been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this," Newsom answered. He described his position as "caution on expanding it, but openness," adding that he believes reforms like term limits are a "no-brainer." HARRIS LABELED 'INSTITUTIONAL ARSONIST' FOR PLAN TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM SCOTUS AND ELECTORAL COLLEGE The California Democrat had harsher criticism of the Electoral College, suggesting that it has "perverted" U.S. politics. "California has already been a leader that's already gone out front saying it's time to change that system. Which state's more burdened by it than my state? We're the size of 21 state populations combined. Come on. And we have two representatives in the Senate? Come on. "And the way that thing favors ... it's perverted, I think, our politics. The Constitution is a living document, and it was conceived to be amended, and I think it's time to make that amendment," Newsom said. Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment. CARVILLE TELLS DEMS TO QUIETLY PREPARE POWER GRAB WITH DC, PUERTO RICO STATEHOOD AND SUPREME COURT PACKING Though Newsom has not explicitly supported expanding the Supreme Court, he made similar comments suggesting an openness to it during an interview with Brian Tyler Cohen on his podcast in June. Cohen was arguing in favor of court expansion, and Newsom remarked that Cohen was "getting me closer to your point of view." During an interview with "PBS NewsHour" on Monday, Newsom also said the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on issues like universal healthcare, climate change and moving off fossil fuels. The DSA's goals include eliminating the Supreme Court and replacing it with a judiciary that would be selected by Congress. House Democrats recently voted against a constitutional amendment to cap the number of justices on the Supreme Court at nine. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who introduced the measure, warned Congress about the downsides of expanding the court. news.title: Susan Collins Faces Fourth Polling Blow Since Jackson Launched Senate Run
news.text: Democrat Troy Jackson held a narrow lead over Republican Senator Susan Collins in a new CNN/SSRS poll of the Maine Senate race published on Wednesday. It’s the fourth consecutive independent poll giving him a lead since he became the Democratic nominee in July. Maine’s Senate race is expected to be one of the most competitive races of the midterms. The Pine Tree State has generally leaned toward Democrats in recent cycles, backing former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024, but Collins has won in the past because of her personal popularity and bipartisan image. The new poll highlights the race's competitive nature as Democrats hope to unseat the longtime incumbent in a national environment shaped by President Donald Trump’s declining national approval rating. Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. Troy Jackson Leads Close Race, CNN Poll Finds Jackson held a 3-point lead over Collins in the new poll, 48 percent to 45 percent. The narrow lead is within the poll’s margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points, so it’s pointing to a very tight race in the state. The poll surveyed 880 registered voters from August 31 to September 6, 2026. The majority (71 percent) of Jackson’s supporters described their vote as being “against Collins,” rather than “for Jackson,” but 74 percent of Collins’ supporters said their vote was “for” the incumbent senator, according to the poll. Jackson’s favorability rating was underwater by 6 points in the poll, with 42 percent viewing him unfavorably and 36 percent viewing him favorably. Collins was 10 points underwater, with 51 percent viewing her unfavorably and 41 percent viewing her favorably. It found a significant gap in the Senate and gubernatorial race, where Democrat Hannah Pingree held a 13-point lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 52 percent to 39 percent. It did not ask about independent candidate Rick Bennett. Collins has outrun other Republicans in Maine in the past. What Other Polls Show The CNN poll aligns with other recent surveys suggesting a close race. An Abacus Data poll released earlier in September found that Jackson led Collins by 9 points, 52 percent to 43 percent among likely voters. But among all registered voters, Collins was up a single point, 46 percent to 45 percent, the poll found. The poll surveyed 500 registered voters and 327 likely voters in Maine from August 26 to 28, 2026. The margin of error among registered voters was plus or minus 4.4 percentage points, but larger among likely voters. A recent Fox News poll showed Jackson up 2 points, 48 percent to 46 percent among 1,000 registered voters. It was conducted from August 6 to 10, 2026 by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. An earlier University of New Hampshire survey gave Jackson a 3-point lead, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,178 likely voters from July 15 to 20, 2026. Can Susan Collins Defy Blue Wave? The Maine Senate race is still considered to be a toss-up by forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball. Polling in the Pine Tree State has been off before. It’s viewed as a harder state to poll because of its older, rural population. The 2020 race between Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon saw a polling error in Collins’ favor, though polling errors are not always duplicated from cycle to cycle. Collins trailed Gideon in nearly every poll but ultimately outperformed the polls to hold onto the seat, even as former President Joe Biden won the state by 9 points that year. Democrats note that 2026 is likely to be a stronger national environment. Voters have soured on the Trump administration amid concerns around the economy, cost of living and the war in Iran. The CNN poll found that 67 percent of Mainers disapprove of Trump, while only 31 percent approve. The state stands to feel the effects of Trump’s latest round of tariffs on Canada. Voters in the state could also face high home heating prices this winter, as many homes there use oil-based heating systems—and oil prices have surged amid the Iran war. Still, Republicans view the race as competitive and have hoped to cast Jackson as too progressive for the state. Democrats have also had a tumultuous election season in the state. Graham Platner, a progressive political newcomer whose campaign garnered national attention, was hit with sexual abuse allegations just weeks after clinching the nomination. He ultimately withdrew from the race but has denied the allegations. Jackson, who initially ran for governor but ultimately lost the primary, emerged as the new nominee during a convention in July, easily securing the required delegates to find his place on the ballot. What Prediction Markets Show Prediction markets favor Jackson to flip Maine. As of Wednesday, he had a 68 percent chance on Kalshi and a 72 percent chance on Polymarket of winning against Collins. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Maine Is Must-Win State for Democrats Democrats’ path to a Senate majority runs through Maine. Overall, Democrats are hoping to flip the Senate but face a tough race. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control if they win every race in a seat they currently hold. Vice President JD Vance serves as the tiebreaker in a split Senate. In order to flip the Senate majority, Democrats have to win every seat they currently hold, flip GOP-held seats in competitive states and win some seats in more traditionally conservative territory. Democrats are defending seats in Trump-won states Georgia and Michigan. In addition to Maine, they view a GOP-held seat in North Carolina as a top flip opportunity. No other Senate races are in Harris-won or single-digit Trump states, meaning Democrats must expand the Senate battleground and compete in more conservative areas if they want to win the majority. They are targeting GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as potential states to flip. The Cook Political Report classifies those four races as toss-ups. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Sam Wilson.

news.title: Trump brings his PT Barnum act to Dallas
news.text:
Welcome to the 2026 Republican midterm convention. Like everything else in the past two years, this is President Donald Trump’s latest scheme to defy history and hold onto the Republican majorities in the House and the Senate.

And he’s made Texas the place where he will make his last stand. He’s poured money into the its Senate race to save his preferred candidate, Ken Paxton. He cajoled Gov. Greg Abbott and the Texas legislature to redraw the congressional map to give Republicans five additional seats. 

If politics is a circus, Trump is doing his best PT Barnum impersonation — only instead of taming a lion, he’s trying to convince a herd of elephants that it’s OK to be dissatisfied with the economy, the price of gas and the costs of nearly everything else so long as Democrats don’t gain control of Congress. 

But in the home of the Dallas Cowboys over the next two nights, Trump is attempting an even bigger Hail Mary by using the never-before-heard-of midterm convention to tout his legislative accomplishments, no matter how thin and unpopular they may be, to the American public. 

And to top it off, Trump announced on Wednesday that he would speak not only on Thursday to close out the bash, but also tonight.

It’s a big contrast for how presidents and their parties typically go about midterms. Historically, members of the president’s party try to create as much distance from the White House as possible, display their independence and appeal to swing voters to make the case. 

And Trump, at 80, is unique in his unpopularity. On Wednesday, an Economist/YouGov poll showed that 42 percent of voters plan to go for the Democratic candidate for Congress compared to 35 percent who plan to vote for the Republican. And only 37 percent of voters approve of Trump’s performance as president. Piling on that, 57 percent of voters without a college degree disapprove of the president.

This might be why for the most part, Republicans in tough House races are avoiding the Dallas convention. Of the candidates in the 37 races that the Cook Political Report rates as either “Lean Democratic,” “Lean Republican” or “Toss-up,” only 10 challengers are speaking at the convention and only six incumbents in battleground races are showing. 

Curiously, Rep. Mike Lawler of New York’s 17th district is the only Republican from a district that voted for Kamala Harris who will speak and many of the incumbent Republicans speaking — such as Reps. Anna Paulina Luna in Florida’s 13th district and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin’s 3rd district — have underperformed Trump. 

But this lays out the central problem for Republicans across the country: As the GOP increasingly becomes the party of non-college-educated voters, it also loses its ability to turn out voters in non-presidential elections. 

Trump typically solves this problem by getting low-trust and low-turnout voters to pull the lever for him, but not for anyone else. As a result, a Trump pep rally might motivate some MAGA voters to turn out in November. But that means they risk losing independents, with whom Trump has only a 25-percent approval rating. 

This poses another problem for the GOP: historically, political conventions have formal duties such as nominating candidates and the opportunity to showcase new talent. With the exception of a few candidates, this will be the Trump show. 

And Trump has even found a way to bigfoot Vice President JD Vance, his would-be heir to MAGA. Instead of setting him up to give the closing speech on the first night, Trump will overshadow his No. 2 just as Vance gets ready to kick the tires on a 2028 presidential run. 

All of this the reminds the GOP that when it comes to the state of the party, Trump has adopted the same approach as WWE legend and Texan, Stone Cold Steve Austin: Arrive, Raise Hell, Leave. 

He has made it impossible for anyone to outshine him. But by making this octogenarian with awful numbers the center of the Republican orbit, the party risks burning their most vulnerable members to a crisp.
news.summary: Trump may be the Republican Party’s greatest showman. But, Eric Garcia writes, his three-ring spectacle risks burning the party to a crisp

news.title: This Could Be a Genius Strategy to Win the Midterms
news.text:
For what it’s worth, there are economic indicators showing the economy is doing much better under Trump. The problem is that gas prices have spiked because of the war in Iran, and that single data point is loud enough to drown out everything else.

But there is a key truth behind any economic message: if voters don’t feel it, you really can’t convince them otherwise. Joe Biden tried and failed to claim that the economy was good on his watch, and people didn’t fall for it because they could see and feel how bad things were at the pump, the grocery store, and on their utility bills.

So what's the Republican Party supposed to do? Well, Trump's 2024 campaign may have already answered that question, just not with the message Republicans are leaning on now.

Trump's closing ads that year didn't rely on economic arguments alone. They used trans issues to paint Kamala Harris as out of touch, with the most memorable campaign ad line declaring, "Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you."

It worked well enough that Democrats are still relitigating it. The 2025 Democrat autopsy called the ad an "irreconcilable problem" precisely because Kamala Harris never abandoned the underlying position it attacked.

Perhaps no ad is more closely associated with the 2024 campaign than the Trump campaign’s anti-transgender spot, with the tagline of “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you.”And the autopsy casts the ad – and Harris’ comments which it was based on – as an irreconcilable problem.It said the campaign’s pollsters “all recognized the attack as very effective.”“If the Vice President would not change her position – and she did not – then there was nothing which would have worked as a response,” the autopsy says.

Elon Musk appears to think that formula still has juice.

Musk's America PAC has launched a large-scale anti-trans ad campaign aimed squarely at the 2026 midterms, and the group isn't pretending it's a persuasion play. It's a get-out-the-vote effort, designed to drive Republican turnout rather than win over anyone still undecided.

ICYMI: After the Lindsay Clancy Verdict, Jurors Are Speaking Out — and Making Things Worse

The targets are specific. New ads are running against four Democrat Senate candidates in competitive races: Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Josh Turek (D-Iowa), James Talarico (D-Texas), and Mary Peltola (D-Alaska). The spots focus on transgender athletes, sex changes for children, and men in women’s locker rooms. The ads are running online and across streaming platforms rather than broadcast television.

This is the first batch of ads America PAC has released for the midterm cycle, and it won't be the last. Musk has reportedly authorized the group to spend as much as $100 million before Election Day.

That's an interesting bet, because trans issues aren’t exactly a top issue of this cycle. Economic concerns dominate voter priorities in poll after poll, while trans and LGBT issues barely register at all. “It's the economy, stupid,” as the saying goes, and no amount of clever ad targeting changes what's sitting at the top of everyone's mind.

But there’s an important caveat here: Musk isn't making the same bet Trump made in 2024. Trump used culture-war messaging to persuade swing voters who hadn't made up their minds. America PAC is using it to make sure Republicans who already agree with the party actually show up when perhaps they are feeling less inclined to do so.

Will it work? I don’t know. But it won’t hurt. If Republicans win in November, I wouldn’t be surprised if this strategy is seen as a factor.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: I went hiking with some Trump supporters. What happened next was surprising
news.text:
I was surprised by the level of vitriol directed at the 2024 Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris by our companions, including falsely claiming she had slept her way to the top. I’d heard this before from my only other Trumpist acquaintance, who followed it up with the claim that Harris wasn’t black. What was Orwell’s warning? That we’d have to deny the evidence of our own eyes and ears? Even more puzzling was that one of our party had a trans daughter who, to her credit, she supported.

Over the next few days, we discovered our companions were lifelong Republicans, so there was something tribal about their political loyalties. I wondered if the rather odd American habit (to this Australian, anyway) of being a registered Republican, Democrat or Independent leads to a my-party-right-or-wrong mentality that I don’t think we see as much of here.

The Americans were also wealthy, and Trump’s economic policies had not affected them. In fact, his bullish sharemarket had made them money.

Two women in our party then revealed that they too had lost adult sons; the grief the little plaque unleashed was real.JANE CARO

There was some self-delusion, in my eyes anyway. They compared Trump to Churchill (they’d just been to the War Cabinet rooms in London), saying both mavericks and unpopular outsiders. There is some truth in that but, despite my good intentions, I couldn’t help point out that Churchill, for all his faults, had won a real Nobel Prize – for literature. I doubt A History of the English-Speaking Peoples can be compared with The Art of the Deal, but maybe that’s just me.
news.summary: You can choose your friends, but not always your travel companions.
news.author: Jane Caro

news.title: Donald Trump Tears Into Kaitlan Collins as Prez Calls CNN Reporter 'Very Dumb and Unhappy' in Fiery Rant
news.text:
President Trump's feud with Kaitlan Collins has ramped up once again, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

Collins hosted a special edition of CNN's The Source titled "Countdown to Election Night," which featured speculation about the upcoming midterm elections in November. The conversation featured a conservative strategist, who opted to speak poorly of Trump.Donald Trump Tears Apart Kaitlan Collins in RantWhile Collins was facilitating the panel, Trump opted to throw low blows her way on Truth Social, calling her "very dumb and unhappy," and claiming she was part of a "fake news" organization.

He claimed the journalist pulled in "really low ratings" for the network, and raged that the panel's "discussions were all FICTION AND LIES."

Trump added, "You would think that CNN, which is suffering terribly in the TV Ratings, would get rid of their 3rd rate 'anchors' and try to bring credibility back to their once-storied network. It is fading FAST! See you all at the Republican National Convention tomorrow night!!! President DJT."Kaitlan Collins' Guest Takes Swipe at PresidentCollins' panel featured conservative strategist Doug Heye, New York Times reporter Shawn McCreesh, NOTUS correspondent Jasmine Wright, and the former communications director to Vice President Kamala Harris, Ashley Etienne.

Despite Heye's right-wing allegiance, he scoffed at Trump's current trajectory. "Donald wants to spend money on himself. He doesn't want to give things away," Heye claimed.

Trump previously called Collins a "corrupt reporter," encouraging her to smile more as she showed "hatred in her eyes."Trump's Previous Feud With Kaitlan CollinsDuring the White House Correspondents' Dinner, which was rescheduled after a gunman entered the building, Trump compared Collins to transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney. 

"I thought Kaitlan Collins had really made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn't her on the Bud Light can; it was Dylan Mulvaney," he said, mocking Mulvaney's sponsorship with Bud Light, which drew immense backlash from the right. 

Trump added, "She never smiles. I said, ‘Kaitlan, do you ever smile? Smile!’ You have a nice position; you're at CNN fake news. You should be a happy person. So smile, Kaitlan! Just smile."

He followed up his comparison by sharing an edited image, morphing Mulvaney and Collins' faces together online.Karoline Leavitt Clashes With Kaitlan CollinsCollins has repeatedly been put down by the Trump administration. She even received quippy feedback from his former press secretary, Karoline Leavitt.

During a press conference, Collins asked Leavitt about American casualties in Iran amid Operation Epic Fury. Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth had previously suggested the press, while reporting on the incident, wanted to "make the president look bad."

Collins pressed Leavitt, asking if Trump's administration backed those comments.

"That's not what the secretary said, Kaitlan, and that's not what the secretary meant – and you know it," Leavitt accused. "You know you are being disingenuous. We've never had a Secretary of Defense who cares more."

news.title: Dems' Agenda Is They/Them II: Musk PAC Enters the Midterms
news.text:
Remember this ad? Elon Musk certainly does:

Many 2024 post-mortems focused on this one attack ad as the fulcrum of Donald Trump's victory. It instantly painted Kamala Harris as an out-of-touch extremist who would obsess over the fringe while ignoring mainstream America. The attack had power because it was based on truth, as even the New York Times was forced to concede at the time. While the election hinged on a number of factors – Harris' general incompetence and incoherence, profligate spending, and the Joe Biden cover-up among them – no attack ad hit harder in that cycle.

Does this attack still have the power to separate the "they/them" from "you and me"? Musk's America PAC plans to lay down a significant amount of money in four key Senate races to test the theory, according to Axios:

Driving the news: In a series of just-launched ads, America PAC goes after Democratic Senate candidates in four competitive races over transgender athletes, gender-transition care and other trans issues.The PAC's emphasis on trans issues is striking because that's been a much less prominent theme in GOP Senate ads so far this election cycle, per AdImpact, which tracks political advertising.The ads, which are running online and on streaming platforms, attack Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Iowa's Josh Turek, Texas' James Talarico and Alaska's Mary Peltola.They're among the first batch of ads from America PAC, which Musk has reportedly authorized to spend upwards of $100 million in the midterms.

To an extent, this is Musk playing defense. Each of these contests is a seat Democrats think they can flip against the GOP in this cycle. Each of them looks relatively close in polling at this point too, although polls in this cycle have performed worse than usual in a predictive sense. (Ask Francesca Wong in Wisconsin where her 20-point lead went.) The first rule in elections is to defend your current seats.

This also makes sense, though, because Democrats in all four states are trying to pretend moderation with radical/progressive candidates. That includes Ohio, where the ad from Musk's super PAC is already running against Sherrod Brown's comeback bid:

New —Elon Musk's super PAC America PAC is going up with its first connected TV ad of the cycle.It's against Sherrod Brown in #OHSen. pic.twitter.com/vEbIc88J9w— Teddy Schleifer (@teddyschleifer) September 8, 2026

Will this be effective in the midterms? Axios' Mike Zapler sounds skeptical:

America PAC's focus on trans issues comes as Republicans face a brutal midterm environment. Voters across party lines are angry about the Iran war and stubbornly high prices that have come with it. ...On its face, the strategy is at odds with what voters say they want candidates to talk about. Concerns about the economy dominate; trans and LGBT issues barely register.

First off, this overlooks some critical context. Candidates can address the economy; super-PACs and other outside groups can work on other issues. But even if these issues do not rank high in issue polls, they may still matter. The WNBA's crisis over biological identity has made headlines for weeks now, thanks to an ESPN reporter who stirred the pot with Sophie Cunningham and touched off a massive paroxysm of grievance politics on the Left. The amplitude of media coverage this summer over Cunningham and her position on biological identity belies the idea that this will be some sort of esoteric issue to the electorate. 

Musk – or at least the people running America PAC – likely see this as an identifier issue for voters. It goes beyond policy to, well, identity, just as it did in 2024. Politicians who play the pronoun game and refuse to oppose pediatric sex-change therapies will stand out like sore thumbs in states like Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, and especially Texas. This is less of an issue ad than it is a values ad, and again, that's exactly how it played two years ago as well. 

That doesn't necessarily mean it will have the same power. However, until it proves otherwise, Musk and his PAC are spending money wisely.
news.author: Ed Morrissey

news.title: Sununu's Chances of Beating Pappas in Knife-Edge New Hampshire Senate Race
news.text: Republican John Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas won their respective primaries on Tuesday, setting up a New Hampshire Senate contest that recent polling shows could be close. The Associated Press has called the Democratic primary for Pappas, with an estimated 89 percent of the vote counted, and the Republican primary for Sununu, with an estimated 85 percent counted. On November 3, New Hampshire voters are set to choose a successor to retiring three-term Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen, and the open seat could influence control of the U.S. Senate. The RealClearPolling average puts Pappas 2 points ahead of Sununu in the general election, while prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket price a Democratic victory at 83 percent. Though forecasters currently give Democrats the advantage, New Hampshire's political history offers encouragement to both nominees. Republicans have not won one of the state's Senate seats since 2010, but Granite State voters remain willing to split their tickets: In 2024, they elected a Republican governor while backing then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the presidential race. Newsweek contacted the Sununu and Pappas campaigns by email for comment on Wednesday morning. Why It Matters Republicans see Sununu—who previously held the seat, has one of the state's best-known political names and received President Donald Trump's endorsement—as a chance to break the GOP's losing streak in New Hampshire Senate elections. Democrats counter that the state has resisted Trump in presidential contests and that the broader political environment favors Pappas. Sponsored by Kalshi Polling Shows NH Senate Race Could Still Move A University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll conducted August 20 to 24 among 1,878 likely voters put Sununu at 45 percent and Pappas at 43 percent. Its margin of error was plus or minus 2.3 percentage points, meaning the Republican's lead was within the survey's sampling error. Another survey taken almost simultaneously pointed the other way. Saint Anselm College polled 1,411 likely voters online from August 17 to 18 and found Pappas ahead 48 percent to 41 percent. That poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points. An earlier Emerson College Polling survey, conducted March 21 to 23 among 1,000 likely voters, found a virtual tie: 45 percent for Pappas and 44 percent for Sununu, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Taken together, the results suggest Sununu has a plausible path but no durable lead. The RealClearPolling average covering March 21 through August 24 placed Pappas at 45.3 percent and Sununu at 43.3 percent, a Democratic edge of 2 points. The electorate also contains sharp demographic crosscurrents, with Emerson College Polling Executive Director Spencer Kimball saying in a news release that women favored Pappas by 9 points and men backed Sununu by 6. Voters younger than 40 supported the Democrat by 23 points, while those in their 50s and 60s preferred the Republican by 12, according to Emerson's survey. Polling, Markets Favor Pappas Close vote shares do not automatically translate into equal winning chances. Prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket are pricing a Democratic victory at 83 percent, with the Republican side at 17 or 18 percent. Prediction markets can react quickly as traders absorb polling, campaign developments and the political environment. Unlike a single survey, their price represents a collective judgment about the eventual winner rather than an estimate of today's vote. Market prices can be moved by limited liquidity, and participants may share the same assumptions. So an 83 percent price is not a guarantee. It means traders regard a Democratic victory as substantially more likely. Traditional forecasters have reached a similar conclusion. As of September 8, Decision Desk HQ rated New Hampshire "Likely Democratic," giving Democrats a 78 percent probability of winning. Cook Political Report classified the race as "Lean Democratic," describing that category as competitive but with one party holding an advantage. Two Familiar Candidates, One Open Seat Pappas, first elected to the House in 2018, is trying to keep the seat in Democratic hands. He comfortably turned back a late challenge from medical scientist Karishma Manzur, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who had gained ground during the closing stretch of the campaign. At the time of writing, Pappas had 65 percent of the vote to Manzur's 32.7 percent, according to AP. Sununu, who served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009, is the son and brother of former New Hampshire governors. At the time of writing, he led former Ambassador Scott Brown 68.6 percent to 26.6 percent. Both the Pappas and Sununu campaigns have already framed the race around Washington influence. In an advertisement, Pappas accused his opponent of siding with pharmaceutical and insurance interests while in Congress before going to work for them and presented himself as a lawmaker "fighting to lower costs." Republican groups, meanwhile, have attacked Pappas over taxes. Alex Latcham, the executive director of the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned super PAC, said in a statement that the organization would promote Sununu's "positive vision for New Hampshire" while challenging the Democrat's record. Democratic strategist Lauren French called Republican confidence in the state "wish-casting," although she acknowledged the contest would be competitive, according to NBC News. Trump’s Picks Win as Shaheen Survives Nail-Biter Tuesday also provided two additional primary-season victories for Trump. Sununu, Trump's endorsed Senate candidate, won the Republican nomination, while Anthony DiLorenzo captured the GOP primary for the 1st Congressional District seat Pappas is leaving behind. On the Democratic side of that House contest, Stefany Shaheen, daughter of the incumbent senator, survived a far more suspenseful evening. The former Portsmouth City Council member defeated New Hampshire Democratic Party Vice Chair Maura Sullivan by a little more than 2 points when Decision Desk HQ called the race at 11:37 p.m. Eastern time. What Happens Next Fresh postprimary polling will show whether voters consolidate along party lines or remain open to splitting their tickets. Until then, the evidence points to a close campaign with an identifiable Democratic favorite, rather than a true fifty-fifty race. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Shakeema Edwards.
news.summary: Polls show a tight New Hampshire Senate race after the primaries, while prediction markets give Democrats the edge.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: Map Shows Rise in Rejected Mail Ballots by Trump, Harris Counties
news.text: A map shows that several Washington counties that backed President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election have seen the biggest surge in the rate of ballots being rejected for late postmarks, fueling concerns that voters will face being disenfranchised in November’s crucial midterm elections. A snapshot report released by Senator Maria Cantwell, a Democrat from Washington, said data from Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs’ office showed that late-postmark rejection rates have more than doubled in 19 counties compared to the 2024 primaries, including in states that backed Trump over former Democratic vice president Kamala Harris in the last presidential election. It comes as changes in USPS policies have raised concerns about voting by mail, particularly in the states where the method is most popular. Trump, a Republican, has repeatedly attacked mail-in voting and claimed that it leads to fraud despite evidence to the contrary and his own repeated use of the method to vote. Other states have also reported an increase in ballots being rejected for late postmarks. Oregon officials announced on Tuesday that 7,314 ballots that arrived in the mail during the state’s seven-day grace period for this year’s May primary were not counted because they were postmarked after Election Day. That meant a rejection rate of 13 percent in this year’s primary, up from 9.5 percent in the 2024 primary. Where Did Rejection Rates Rise the Most? The report said that rate of ballots rejected for late postmarks increased by 32 percent in Washington state’s August primary compared to the 2024 primary. According to the data, the five counties that saw the biggest surge in the late-postmark rejection rates between the 2024 and 2026 primaries all backed Trump in 2024. Mason County recorded a 329.7 percent increase, followed by Stevens County with 303.7 percent, Yakima County with 268.5 percent, Okanogan County with 263.5 percent and Franklin County at 206 percent. But while the biggest surges were concentrated in Republican-leaning counties, some counties that were won by Harris also saw a substantial increase in the rate of ballots discounted for late postmarks. Clallam County saw a 199 percent increase in ballots rejected for late postmarks between the 2024 and 2026 primaries, while Whitman County saw a 133.2 percent increase. Snohomish County, which also backed Harris, saw an increase of 66.9 percent. Rise in Rejection Rates Attributed to USPS Rules At a news conference earlier in September, Cantwell attributed the increase in ballot rejection rates to changes in USPS policies and said they have led to significant voter disenfranchisement in her state, particularly in rural areas. She also noted that Trump may be disenfranchising some of his own supporters. "I find a little bit of irony here that the president may be disenfranchising his most stable voters in rural communities by taking the vote away," she said. In December, USPS finalized a rule clarifying that postmarks don’t necessarily reflect the date the agency first took possession of a piece of mail, but the day it was handled in one of its processing centers. That raised questions about mail-in ballots, which in some states depend on a postmark date to determine if a vote counts. If a ballot is dropped into a mailbox on Election Day but not processed by a sorting machine until later, the postmark could indicate a date after the legal deadline. USPS also implemented a new policy last year that mail will only be transported once a day, rather than twice, from post offices or collection boxes that are more than 50 miles from a postal distribution center. In a statement to The Associated Press, USPS acknowledged that changes in how it transports mail could result in postmarking delays. Anyone who wants to ensure their ballots are postmarked on time can go into a post office and ask for it to be stamped manually for free, it said. "Our consistent message to voters who choose to vote by mail is to mail early"—at least one week before ballots are due, the statement said. Newsweek has contacted Cantwell's office and USPS for further comment via email. Cantwell Calls for Senate Hearing Cantwell urged her colleagues in the Senate to hold hearings on the issue. "I'm calling on my colleagues in the United States Senate to do their oversight job and hold hearings as why the president of the United States and the United States Postal Service is disenfranchising voters across the United States with policies that are leaving them with a ballot that was cast but never counted," Cantwell said. She added: "We're just 62 days away from a pivotal midterm election. And our report shows some troubling trends. Ballots that voters believed they had mailed in time were rejected because they lacked a timely verifiable postmark or arrived too late to be counted." Cantwell explained that the issue is worse in rural counties where voters may not be able to easily reach ballot drop boxes. "If you are now casting your ballot, driving to that post office, who's not stamping your ballot as received and stamped that day? That's what Washingtonians need to know: the post office is taking your ballot as a piece of mail, but not stamping it that day." That’s important, she said, because almost a third of voters "wait until the last 48 hours to vote." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Cannon and Robert Greenall
news.summary: Data shows the rate of mail ballots rejected for arriving late surged in Washington counties that voted for Donald Trump in 2024.
news.author: Khaleda Rahman

news.title: Surprise! These top AI bots are politically left wing
news.text:
A systems engineer prompted a slew of AI bots to take the Political Compass test online to determine where their answers landed on the political spectrum between the right and the left. To absolutely no one’s surprise, most of the bots fell onto the left side of the map with only one in the center, leaning right. Any guesses which one?

The Political Compass is an exam comprising 62 propositions designed to reveal the political ideology of the person taking the test. Instead of people, though, a systems engineer based in Denmark who goes by the name Zapador had a whole host of AI bots take the test. Among the frontier candidates were ChatGPT by OpenAI, Claude by Anthropic, Gemini by Google, Grok by SpaceXAI, plus many more.

AI platforms with political opinions will have an effect on the conclusions people draw and the opinions they form.

To ensure that the results were as accurate as possible, Zapador had each bot take the test “at least five times” before plotting their average scores on a graph. The results are included below.

 AI Political Compass Test Results/aipolcom.net

The numbers don’t lie

As you can see, most of the AI bots fell well within the left libertarian category. In fact, only one AI bot differed significantly. The two gray dots on the center libertarian line and the single dot in the right libertarian section represent three versions of Grok — Grok 4.3 is most right-leaning, Grok 4.5 is next, and Grok 4.6 is closest to the line.

Looking at the other side, Google Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with no reasoning was the farthest left out of the mainstream options tested, followed by open-weight models Gemma 4 31B and GPT-OSS 120B.

Needless to say, if you’re looking for an AI bot that takes a balanced-to-right-leaning approach to its responses, Grok’s latest models are the only options on the table.

Unfortunately, when looking at global market share based on website traffic, Grok only accounts for 2.4% of the AI market. news.text:

news.title: GOP's Midterm Convention: Narrative Changer?
news.text:
Tonight, the RNC and Donald Trump will launch a grand experiment in American politics. Republicans will kick off a two-day midterm convention, an innovation in a political system that may be the most honest reckoning of what conventions actually are in a very long time. It has two purposes, but the big dice roll is whether a two-day media event can recast the narrative of a midterm cycle.

Fortunately for Republicans, Democrats have given them plenty of assistance on that objective. And in more ways than one.

First, though, Damian Paletta offers this curtain-raiser on the convention itself for the Wall Street Journal. After the obligatory 'Welcome to Dallas' and coverage notes, Paletta breaks out the major events scheduled for the next two days. Note well that Trump himself will offer speeches on both nights, a recognition of his role in the party as well as his push for the convention itself:

Trump: Eleven years after he first rode down the golden escalator, Trump is still the center of gravity in the Republican Party. Even with poor poll numbers, he is the most powerful figure in the party. Trump will give the keynote address Wednesday and then the closing remarks Thursday as the convention works to put him on full display. Vice President JD Vance will speak Thursday before Trump.Democratic divisions: The GOP is expected to play up the leftward lunge that a number of Democratic candidates have made during the primary season. They will attempt to paint the Democrats as dangerous and out of step with mainstream America. Winning this argument could be key to the GOP success in November. Democrats will be stirring the pot, though. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 presidential candidate for the Democrats, will be speaking in Dallas on Wednesday not far from the big convention.

First off, it's worth discussing the entire format. The GOP may be doing some party business in Dallas, but this is not a "convention" in the traditional sense of a presidential nominating process. Of course, the quadrennial conventions stopped being about that process quite a long time ago, too. The last open convention where a nomination was even arguably at risk was the 1984 Democrat convention, where Walter Mondale narrowly avoided an open convention in the final days of the primaries. (Republicans had a real open convention in 1976.) 

Democrats stripped the mask off in 2024. Faced with an actual nominating crisis weeks before their convention, with Joe Biden's senility exposed on national TV, the party had an obvious mechanism to choose another nominee: its "nominating convention" in mid-August. Rather than give delegates their opportunity to perform the nominal duty of that role, party leaders instead anointed Kamala Harris as the nominee and closed ranks to prevent a floor fight at their convention. It made very clear that at least one major party saw its convention as nothing more than a messaging platform, and its delegates as nothing more than accessories. 

So why not do this in the midterms too? It's a smart play, although it certainly will cost a few million dollars to stage it. 

It's especially smart for Trump. Normally, midterms are referenda on the current president, and Trump is not exactly at his popular peak at the moment. Trump is gambling that he can turn the "Democratic divisions" narrative into the major storyline of the midterms with two days of pounding his opponents as radicals and Marxists. 

And this is where Democrats have made it easy, because they nominated radicals and Marxists for House and Senate seats. As I have written repeatedly, this isn't a Red Scare – it's a Code Red. Outright Marxists and barely-crypto-Marxists are running for the US Senate, House, and gubernatorial seats in states like Florida, Michigan, Maine, Wisconsin, and Texas. The GOP needs to nationalize those races and force all other Democrats to answer for their party's radical turn, and a two-night national convention provides a short-cut to implementing that Akin Strategy in every contest.

Moreover, Democrats seem to have been caught with their pants down. Pritzker giving a speech in Dallas is hardly an effective counterprogramming strategy against a massive media event on the scale of the GOP's midterm convention. James Talarico is supposedly doing an event tonight or tomorrow in an attempt to distract people from Dallas, too, which again exposes a lack of scale in Democrat strategic thinking. They might have done better to just hunker down for a couple of days and pretend it wasn't happening; these responses are not only weak, they project weakness. And Talarico himself is one of the more extreme nominees that will get lots of attention from this convention tonight and tomorrow, too. 

Will it work? Again, it's a gamble, but given the stakes, it's a relatively cheap gamble. The convention will allow Republicans to boost their esprit de corps ahead of the political battles ahead, which helps even if the narratives don't shift as planned. The real question will be whether Republicans have the gastric fortitude to keep the focus on Democrats' embrace of radical Marxism, and whether voters recognize its dangers. On that point, they can't claim not to have been warned if Republicans follow through properly.

We will live blog both nights of the convention here at Hot Air, with all of our writers (and perhaps our contributors) on hand. Our live blog will begin at 7 PM ET, so join us for the ride!

Republicans have seized on previous comments he's made on issues like veganism and gender, claiming he's too extreme for Texas, but it remains to be seen whether voters agree. 

The Cook Political Report and University of Virginia's Center for Politics rate the race as a toss-up.

Iowa: Josh Turek vs. Ashley Hinson

GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek will face off in November to represent Iowa in the Senate after GOP Sen. Joni Ernst announced she wouldn't seek reelection, opening up what's become a surprisingly competitive race in a state that's shifted to the right in recent years. 

After Ernst's announcement, Republicans quickly rallied behind Hinson, 43, who has represented Iowa in the House since 2021. The former local news anchor has the president's endorsement and has vowed to be his "top ally" in the Senate, while campaigning on issues like healthcare, veterans benefits, and fighting corruption. 

Turek, 47, is a state representative and former wheelchair basketball Paralympian. And as he aims to flip Iowa's Senate seat blue this cycle, he's touting his history as the Democrat representing the most conservative district in the state. On the campaign trail, he points to his record of working across the aisle and pledges to work with the president. 

Although Iowa hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, and Mr. Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024, Democrats have been hopeful about their chances, as affordability issues and the Trump tariff policies weigh on Iowans. Democrats also hope that a strong showing from Auditor Rob Sand in the governor's race could buoy Turek in November. It will be challenging for a Democrat to flip the seat in a state that's become a Republican stronghold in recent years. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up, while the University of Virginia's Center for Politics ranks it as leaning Republican.

Georgia: Jon Ossoff vs. Mike Collins

GOP Rep. Mike Collins is taking on Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia in a competitive race that was once expected to be the easiest pickup opportunity for Republicans. 

Ossoff is the sole Democrat seeking reelection in a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024. But a messy Republican primary blunted efforts to launch the general election fight to unseat the first-term senator. 

Collins, 59, became the Republican nominee in June after the primary went to a runoff. The owner of a trucking business, Collins has represented Georgia in the House since 2023, and has pitched himself in the Senate race as a staunch ally of the president, while touting his sponsorship of an immigration bill named for Georgia nursing student Laken Riley. At the same time, he's cast Ossoff as out of touch with Georgian values. But his campaign has also been marked with controversies surrounding people in Collins' circle, including a former staffer who reportedly shared Nazi and KKK images on social media. 

Ossoff, 39, first came to the Senate in 2021, after previously working as a staffer on Capitol Hill and in investigative journalism. At the time, he delivered Democrats one of two runoff victories in Georgia, securing the party's control of the chamber. Now, Ossoff, a possible 2028 White House hopeful, is fighting to hold onto the seat in a state that shifted toward the right during the last election. 

Georgians haven't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2016. And Democrats see Collins' closeness to the president as a possible boon for Ossoff amid the unpopular war with Iran and other White House policies. The Cook Political Report rates the race as leaning Democrat, while the University of Virginia's Center for Politics rates the race as likely Democrat.

New Hampshire: Chris Pappas vs. John Sununu

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former GOP Sen. John Sununu are vying for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen opted not to seek reelection in the Granite State.

Pappas, 46, has represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019. He's billed himself as an independent voice and campaigned on his record in Congress, where he's a member of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus.

Sununu, 61, represented New Hampshire in the House and Senate for more than a decade, before he was ousted by Shaheen. The son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu, his name carries significant weight in New Hampshire.

New Hampshire hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, and a Republican hasn't won in the state at the presidential level since 2000. But Republicans have controlled the governor's mansion since 2017. The Cook Political Report and the University of Virginia's Center for Politics rate the race as leaning Democrat.

North Carolina: Michael Whatley vs. Roy Cooper 

Former Gov. Roy Cooper and former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley will face off in North Carolina in November after Sen. Thom Tillis announced he wouldn't seek reelection, opening up a key seat in the competitive state. 

The Tar Heel State offers a key prize for Democrats, representing their best chance at flipping a seat this cycle. And the party secured their dream recruit in Cooper, 69, a two-term governor and the longest-serving state attorney general in North Carolina's history.

Whatley, 57, has never run for office. He worked in former President George W. Bush's administration and as chief of staff for former North Carolina Sen. Elizabeth Dole before serving as chairman of the state Republican Party and going on to play a key role in Mr. Trump's reelection effort as RNC chair. He entered the Senate race with the president's encouragement and has campaigned on helping enact Mr. Trump's agenda and fighting for conservative values. 

North Carolina hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 2008, the same year voters in the state last supported a Democrat at the presidential level. But Democrats think Cooper can break that streak. 

The Cook Political Report and the University of Virginia's Center for Politics rate the race as leaning Democrat.

Minnesota: Peggy Flanagan vs. Michele Tafoya

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya are vying for an open Senate seat representing Minnesota, after Democratic Sen. Tina Smith opted not to seek reelection in the North Star state.

Flanagan, 46, is the lieutenant governor and a former state representative. She won the Democratic primary in August against a more moderate candidate, running on progressive priorities like Medicare for All and securing endorsements from the likes of Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. 

Tafoya, 61, beat out a crowded field for the GOP nomination. She's campaigned on restoring accountability as multimillion-dollar fraud schemes have rattled the state. And although Minnesota hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2002, the GOP is hoping to make inroads as they seek to hold onto control of the chamber next year, seeing some opportunity in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won by just four points in 2024. 

Republicans see a possible winning argument with Flanagan being tied to the Minnesota governor's handling of the fraud schemes in the state. But Minnesota has also been at the center of the Trump administration's controversial immigration crackdown, which saw the fatal shootings of two American citizens by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. The homeland security policies played a big role in the Democratic primary and will likely remain top of mind in November.

The Cook Political Report and the University of Virginia's Center for Politics rate the race as likely Democrat.

Kansas: Roger Marshall vs. Adam Hamilton

GOP Sen. Roger Marshall is defending his seat in a race that has appeared to become surprisingly competitive in recent months amid a challenge from Rev. Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat. 

Marshall, 66, is seeking a second term in the Senate after representing Kansas in the House since 2017. The fifth-generation Kansan is a medical doctor who worked for 25 years as an OB-GYN and served in the U.S. Army Reserves before coming to Capitol Hill, where he's been a reliable supporter of the president's agenda.

Hamilton, 62, is also a fifth-generation Kansan who leads the U.S.' largest United Methodist church. He's running on an affordability-focused agenda, while aiming to bring together a cross-party coalition to take on Marshall. And as a well-known author and speaker, his high profile and fundraising chops have made him a formidable opponent. 

Kansas last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1932. But the Sunflower state has regularly oscillated between electing Democrats and Republicans in gubernatorial races in recent decades, and currently has a Democrat in the governor's mansion.

The Cook Political Report and University of Virginia's Center for Politics rate the race as likely Republican.

Nebraska: Pete Ricketts vs. Dan Osborn

Independent candidate Dan Osborn is making a second attempt to unseat a Republican incumbent in Nebraska's Senate race this year, after losing his bid by single digits in 2024. 

Osborn, 51, a former union leader lost to GOP Sen. Deb Fischer by seven points in 2024. Now he's attempting to unseat Sen. Pete Ricketts, the former Nebraska governor who was appointed to the Senate in 2023. Ricketts, 62, easily won his bid in a special election last year to serve out the remaining two years of Sen. Ben Sasse's term.

Osborn has said if he wins, he would remain independent and does not plan to caucus with either Republicans or Democrats.

Nebraskans haven't elected a candidate who wasn't a Republican since 2006, and the state is solidly red. But it's also home to a large share of nonpartisan voters, who could make the race within striking distance for Osborn, given that the Democratic candidate withdrew from the race. The Cook Political Report and University of Virginia's Center for Politics rate the race as likely Republican.

news.title: The establishment strikes back in New Hampshire Senate primary
news.text:
The political establishment has carried the day in the Senate primary elections in New Hampshire.

U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) won the Democratic nomination on Tuesday to succeed three-term Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, while former Sen. John Sununu captured the Republican nomination, setting up an open-seat general election critical to both parties’ hopes of running the Senate.

'I'm New Hampshire.'

With nearly 88% of the expected vote counted, establishment favorite Pappas crushed socialist Karishma Manzur 65% to 33%, with the remaining Democrat vote split among David Jarvis, Maxwell Saal, and John Vail.

Sununu faced a challenge from former Massachusetts senator and Trump administration alum Scott Brown, but ultimately beat him 68.5% to 26.7%. Several other Republicans finished in the distant single digits. 

New Hampshire has not elected a Republican senator since 2010, but August University of New Hampshire polling shows Sununu leading Pappas 45% to 43%. 

“We’re taking nothing for granted, this is a purple state,” Pappas told MS NOW. “We’ve got a path to victory. But it’s going to be a tough race.”

Former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the Granite State by just three points in 2024, with all 10 counties shifting right since 2020. 

RELATED: Is the DSA about to scalp another establishment Democrat?

 Mel Musto/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Pappas has represented New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District since 2019 and served on the state’s Executive Council from 2013 to 2019. He is co-owner of his family’s Puritan Backroom restaurant. Pappas received endorsements from Sens. Shaheen and Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) and Kamala Harris. 

Pappas raised over $15 million during the primary campaign, dwarfing Manzur’s $415,081. Manzur tacked far to Pappas’ left, repeatedly accusing him of being a pro-Israel stooge and corporate cut-out. 

“Chris Pappas’ hypocrisy is evident. He talks about getting big money out of politics, then turns around and takes bribes from special interests,” a Manzur campaign spokesperson previously told Blaze News. “He talks about standing up to Netanyahu, yet he has voted to send billions of our tax dollars to support Netanyahu’s war."

On the Republican side, Sununu served in the House from 1997 to 2003 and the Senate from 2003 to 2009. His father and brother were both governors of New Hampshire. 

“I’m New Hampshire. I said in my campaign announcement that I’ll have one job: standing up for New Hampshire every single day,” Sununu told the Dartmouth when asked about his primary challenger Scott Brown. “I’m not focused on another office or currying favor with anyone outside this state.

Brown previously served as senator from 2010 to 2013 after winning the special election prompted by the death of Sen. Ted Kennedy (D-Mass.). Brown supported Trump in 2016, netting him an ambassadorship to New Zealand and Samoa.

Sununu received President Donald Trump’s endorsement despite authoring a 2024 op-ed titled “Donald Trump is a loser” in support of Nikki Haley’s 2024 presidential campaign. Sununu later walked back the barb by saying the publication Union Leader chose the headline. 

A UNH poll headed into Primary Election Day showed Sununu leading Brown 60% to 20%.

news.title: Incumbent New Hampshire Republican shrugs off primary challengers in win for purple-state moderates
news.text:
Incumbent New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte secured the Republican nomination for a second two-year term on Tuesday, beating two outsider candidates and teeing up a November battle against Democrat nominee Cinde Warmington. 

With about 84% of expected votes counted, Ayotte won 91.6% of the Republican vote, trouncing Shaun Fife’s 4.1% and Bob Wayne McClory’s 3.5%, according to NBC News. Warmington advanced to the general election automatically as the only Democrat on the ballot. 

'No income tax, no sales tax. Not now, not EVER!'

Ayotte previously served as U.S. senator from 2011 to 2017, losing her re-election bid to former Gov. Maggie Hassan in 2016 by about 1,000 votes. Ayotte defeated former Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig in 2024 to become governor. 

Ayotte didn’t run as a culture warrior in 2024. New Hampshire went for then-Vice President Kamala Harris by three points but has kept a Republican trifecta in its state government since 2021. Republicans also control the state’s Executive Council, a unique governing body that shares executive power with the governor. 

University of New Hampshire polling conducted in August put Ayotte’s approval rating at 49%, with 42% disapproval. 

The incumbent’s campaign has focused on kitchen table issues, emphasizing public safety policy and low taxes. New Hampshire is one of the few states without its own income or sales tax, and Ayotte plans to keep it that way.

RELATED: Deadlines are fast approaching on Trump's mail-in ballot initiatives as election season begins

 CJ Gunther/Getty Images

"I've said it before, and I will say it again," Ayotte said in a March X post. "No income tax, no sales tax. Not now, not EVER!" 

She also promised to address rising housing costs through regulatory changes and collaboration with the Republican-controlled legislature.

Those cost-of-living concerns are a top issue for Granite State voters, according to August UNH polling, as are housing affordability and property taxes. 

Ayotte has also touted her controversial keystone Education Freedom Accounts, which let parents spend the state’s per-pupil aid on homeschooling or private education rather than public school. 

Ayotte’s Republican opponents didn’t mount serious campaigns. Gilmanton farmer Shaun Fife, who took just 0.6% of the vote in the 2024 gubernatorial primary, refused donations and promoted alternative currencies and monetary systems. 

Bob Wayne McClory also finished with 0.6% of the vote in the 2024 primary. McClory did not fundraise or make public comments during the 2026 primary. 

Democrats, by contrast, closed ranks early.

Though Warmington ran unopposed this cycle, she unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic nomination in 2024. Warmington is a health care attorney and served as an executive councilor from 2021 to 2025. 

Warmington is campaigning against Ayotte’s Education Freedom Accounts, blaming them for driving up property taxes. She has also slammed ICE and promised to fight Donald Trump, though she notably agrees with Ayotte that New Hampshire should not enact a state income or sales tax.

The health care attorney has drawn fire from both sides of the aisle for working with Purdue Pharma as an opioid lobbyist from 2001 to 2002.

“What I did not know at the time was that Purdue Pharma was engaged in this massive criminal fraud, something that would be exposed only over years of litigation, that they convinced doctors that it was safer to prescribe Oxycontin under circumstances when it was not,” Warmington said in an August video. 

Warmington is supported by Planned Parenthood NH Action, Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who is now running for Senate. 

Ayotte has been endorsed by the Professional Fire Fighters of New Hampshire and Turning Point Action. 

Multiple general-election polls conducted in August showed Ayotte leading Warmington roughly 49-39.
