news.title: Testosterone, Divorce, and Big-Ass Trucks: On the Trail With James Talarico and Ken Paxton
news.text:
He is “clearly transitioning into a female,” reported White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller. He was a “gay vegan,” Fox News host Jesse Watters added. A Republican National Committee spokesperson charged that he “might still sleep in a kid’s-sized bed with sheets from his favorite Disney princess.” Paxton himself, 63, called his opponent “Low-T Talarico.” Reporters dutifully took this to the state legislator: Did he have low testosterone? “I don’t think guys my age are really concerned about that kind of thing,” Talarico, 37, said.
Picking through this distraction campaign is mostly counterproductive, but I’m going to try, because of the obvious ignorance on display about Texas manhood. Let’s start with the taco. In May, Talarico went to a taco joint in Austin with Barack Obama and got two potato, egg, and cheese breakfast tacos. See? A vegan! Republicans cried, though it was a vegetarian order. “Eggs and cheese aren’t going to get you any Latino voters,” said a CNN This Morning With Audie Cornish panelist. “Clearly not,” said Cornish. This was all profoundly embarrassing. Papas con huevo is one of the most popular taco orders in the state.
Then there was the photo of Talarico eating barbecue. “He is holding that rib with a FREAKING NAPKIN. They just don’t get it,” said Cynical Publius (one of those guys on X with a Roman-statue avatar and hundreds of thousands of followers). But the picture was—as any Texan could have determined through context clues—of Talarico eating a turkey leg at the State Fair of Texas, where it is served wrapped in paper.
Finally, the campaign released a photo of Talarico and his hot girlfriend at Austin City Limits. Haters seized on a new point: Talarico went to a music festival in a white button-down shirt? Kind of a nerd, wouldn’t you say? Context had collapsed again. He was wearing a Columbia fishing shirt—affordable, vented for the heat—meaningfully more “authentic” than the Marine Layer polo a newer Austin transplant might wear. “I don’t wear no Stetson,” sings Terry Allen on his 1979 double album, Lubbock (On Everything), “but I’m willing to bet, son, that I’m as big a Texan as you are.”
The Texas Senate race has enormous implications for the state (it is the Democrats’ best chance in nearly three decades at overturning the Republican monopoly on power) and for the country (inasmuch as control of the Senate could determine how Trump’s presidency will come to an end). So it seems only natural that the race would devolve into schoolyard shenanigans. I followed both campaigns to Texas’s southern border to unpack the question that is, at the end of the day, being asked in November: Do the chuds own Texas, like they say they do—or can the state be something, anything, else?
“Why did you cheat on your wife?” asked the woman caller. “Um,” began Ken Paxton. We were assembled for a Paxton telephone town hall, and this could hardly be said to be an unfair question: In some ways it was the most obvious one.
Paxton is in the middle of a divorce from state senator Angela Paxton, who was his strongest supporter as he ascended from one office to another. Back in 2014, when he ran for attorney general of Texas, she penned a song—“I’m a pistol-packin’ mama, and my husband sues Obama,” she sings—and performed it at rallies. When Angela joined the Texas Senate in 2019, she wrote a bill to legalize the financial crimes for which Ken had been indicted in 2015—which, even in Texas, took some real balls. (It was killed before it went to a vote.) In 2022, when a process server tried to serve him a subpoena at his house, Angela was the getaway driver as Ken fled in a truck.
Last year, she shocked the state by announcing she was seeking separation on “biblical grounds.” Paxton began traveling with a Christian influencer from Louisiana. No weapon formed against him prospered, to put it biblically.
But Paxton, on this call, didn’t seem to have ever considered an answer—he acted surprised to have been asked. He had been slow to start campaigning and took a trip to London for the July Fourth holiday weekend. His operating system seemed to spin and then reboot. “I’m not going to talk about personal issues that relate to my family, just like I don’t think you would want to discuss your marriage on a call with thousands of people,” he said, before a staffer eventually rescued him.
Paxton’s spokesperson, Madison Cercy, told GQ: “We are declining to comment and fully expect this profile will remind Texans of your attempt to position Beto O’Rourke as ‘Kennedy-esque’ when he was running against Ted Cruz. Texans will see right through your glowing piece. James Talarico will lose just like Beto did and become the butt of jokes like him too. As much as you try to mask his weakness, James Talarico is the leftist socialist who will never be able to represent the majority of Texans.”
Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 Senate campaign is the natural point of comparison for Talarico’s run. O’Rourke’s charisma, which surfaced through his long, livestreamed wanderings of the state, combined with Trump’s midterm unpopularity, carried the Democrat to within three percentage points of victory against incumbent Ted Cruz. Though nobody ever went broke underestimating the Democratic Party in Texas, it doesn’t seem unrealistic to think that the state could have moved three points left in the past eight years, with the national climate having gotten much worse for Republicans.
Stylistically, however, the two Democrats couldn’t be more different. O’Rourke came up in the El Paso punk scene and ran a DIY campaign, swinging at hard pitches—a question about Colin Kaepernick’s protests, for example—in his raucous town halls. Because the idea of a Democrat winning in Texas was self-evidently ridiculous, he could kind of just do it. In Marfa, the high-desert art mecca, I was with his campaign at a rally at the glamping hotel El Cosmico. He sat down to talk to me over a beer and ended the night talking at length with an adobe craftsman who, because he was a Mexican national on a worker visa, could not actually vote for him. We might never see a campaign like it again. But he got close.
And because O’Rourke got close, the idea of winning is not that ridiculous anymore, and now Talarico is running a somewhat conventional purple-state campaign with traditional message discipline—affordability, security, opportunity. These are skills he developed in the legislature by questioning Republicans about illogical bills, clipping videos of the interrogations, and hoping they’d go viral on social media. He’s a planner, not an improviser.
I was with the Talarico campaign partway through its 750-mile swing from El Paso to McAllen, which makes up more than a third of the US-Mexico border. I hadn’t been to far-west Texas with a candidate since O’Rourke’s run. I was slow therefore to recognize the scritching sound that occurred when I was poking around the bushes. A diamondback rattlesnake, maybe four feet long, obligingly slithered away from my feet.
We were in Alpine, a town of 6,000 beset by critical failures in its water-distribution system. The campaign party had come down a long rocky road to look at the community’s efforts to drill an emergency well. The mayor told Talarico and his filming team, diplomatically, that the state’s congressional delegation hadn’t been much help. She didn’t say that the district’s current congressman was retiring, his career ruined after one of his staffers, with whom he had allegedly had an affair, died after setting herself on fire last year—or that his likely replacement was Brandon Herrera, a “guntuber” who cracks jokes about the Holocaust. A person at the event suggested Talarico should run for president next. Talarico let it pass by. The video team made sure to get the rattlesnake.
In nearby Marfa, Talarico’s campaign had arranged a rally at the Thunderbird Hotel. Tightly orchestrated, mostly on time. The candidate’s stump was polished, relatively brief, and didn’t vary much from town to town. He spoke about his love for his great-grandfather, whom he calls Poppy, who returned from fighting fascism in WW II to model the honor of service and the teachings of Jesus Christ. There were hundreds of people present, in a town of about 2,000, and the photo line curled around three sides of the large room.
I decided to talk to the two most visually dissimilar men in the audience. The first was Jerry Mitchell, a retired homebuilder, who came from Alpine. Big cowboy hat, white ranch shirt, clean boot-cut blue jeans, black boots, wiry build. A man who’s seen some sun. Had he voted for Democrats often? “Lately,” he said, in a low voice, “you gotta vote for the woman.” (He seemed to be referring to Kamala Harris or Hillary Clinton, not Talarico.) Decent Republicans, he said, “and there’s a lot of them, they’re just not gonna vote in this race.”
If Paxton’s “runnin’ around on his wife,” Mitchell said in a fine twang, “that’s his business.” The problem was “he’s become a millionaire while he’s in office, on a state salary.” In Texas, this is not a crime per se—little is, in the way of political corruption. But the Trumpian masculinity of getting away with it isn’t considered a good look, either.
Across the room was Dillon Orr, 27. Black boots, black skinny jeans, black denim jacket, long black hair, black leather wrist bandolier decorated with ammo cartridges. He is named after Dillon Aero, manufacturer of the M134D Minigun, he told me. He is a docent at the nearby Chinati Foundation contemporary art museum and a former telescope operator at the McDonald Observatory. He makes leather goods and builds hot rods—among them Angel, a souped-up Pontiac Firebird Trans Am, all black also, with exhaust pipes fanned up on the side like wings. “This Machine Kills Fascists” is painted on the back.
“Someone who pardons rapists, that’s not masculine in any way,” Orr said. (Paxton’s office has drawn criticism for lenient plea deals in cases involving sex trafficking and child sex abuse.) “That’s not doing the male job of protecting you’re supposed to do.” J.R.R. Tolkien was a veteran, Orr pointed out, and the father of veterans. Didn’t he have Lord of the Rings character Faramir say, as Orr paraphrased, “I love the bright sword, not for its sharpness of steel or its ability to kill, but for that which it can defend?” When I peeked inside Angel, on my way out, there was a longsword on the back seat.
A few days later, in McAllen, Paxton held his Rally in the Valley at a steamy outdoor venue. He was endorsed by the National Border Patrol Council and appeared with various south Texas bigwigs. The Paxton campaign’s focus on macho, it has been widely reported, is aimed at voters here, at the southern tip of the state, in former Democratic strongholds where in 2024 Hispanic voters, particularly men, swung to Trump.
Talarico had been able to notch a small win on the border, in far-off Big Bend, where a handful of sheriffs who oppose the construction of the wall through their iconic landscape appeared at Talarico’s rally, though they stopped short of endorsing him. Paxton’s friends were less reticent. Tano Tijerina, current congressional candidate and a former judge in Webb County, home to Laredo, introduced Paxton. Tijerina looks a bit like Dave Bautista. A wrestler’s build, big bald head covered by a bigger white hat, a forceful personality. Tijerina said he was a “beef-eating, Bible-thumping patriot.” The crowd got riled.
But Paxton seemed unsure of himself and the crowd. “So, what are the differences between me and my opponent? I’m sure you know some of them,” he said. “One of them is family. Actually…let me talk about faith first. Faith.” Talarico was a fake Christian, he said, who wanted to genitally mutilate children. (Talarico voted against a bill to ban gender-reassignment surgery for minors; he has lately argued that he opposed that bill because it was too broad, and he generally opposes the procedure for children.) Paxton did not talk much about his own faith, or his own family.
I might not be a prince, his campaign seemed to say, but the other fellow isn’t even a man. Over the summer, Paxton’s camp pointed out that Talarico shared a joint checking account with his mother. A bit embarrassing, maybe. But this attack, like others on Talarico’s masculinity, changes meaning depending on one’s expectations. State representatives like Talarico make less than $8,000 a year, and, in Texas, there are a thousand different legal ways of paying off a lawmaker. To be a broke legislator, you have to be one of two things: stupid or honest.
When I caught Talarico for a one-on-one in August, he seemed to be putting the summer’s virility debate in the rearview, tightly focused on the buzzword of the cycle: affordability. Watching Paxton talk about affordability, Talarico told me, “it’s kind of like watching him speak French or something.” Paxton wants to offer tax deductions for second homes, medical bills, and gym memberships, Talarico said, even though some of the major factors driving price increases are tariffs and the war in Iran, and the preferences given to special interests and billionaires. “I’m mystified,” he said. “A lot of people in my family, a lot of my friends, voted for President Trump in 2024 because of this issue of prices…and instead of lowering prices, he decided to start a new forever war in the Middle East.”
But “when Ken Paxton started all this talk about who’s a real man,” Talarico said, “I decided to engage with it.” The terrain was too important to cede, he felt, even if it had been inlaid with cringe-inducing traps. Such as when, in July, the Talarico campaign released an ad showing the candidate ripping down a country road in a big-ass Dodge Ram—a rental, it turned out. Talarico’s own white Chevy Colorado, a truck disdained by Truck Guys for its diminutive stature, has tinted windows that made filming difficult, the campaign said.
Still, when Talarico gets going on the influence of his adoptive father, he can be genuinely moving. “The luckiest day in my life was when I met Mark Talarico, who fell in love with my mom and fell in love with me and gave me his last name, which I’m very proud to have on these campaign signs all over the state,” he said. “He took responsibility. He raised me as his own.”
He hopes that young men are “hungry for an alternative” to manosphere masculinity. Even if culture is telling them masculinity is something to be consumed and acquired—here I’ll paraphrase: eat beef, hustle and grind, get a better wife—he thinks they also know, deep down, “real men don’t lie and cheat their way through life.”
In Eagle Pass, a sun-drenched working-class border town, Talarico gave his familiar, polished stump speech, speaking in the round. Then he took questions. Each one offered up some explicit, or implicit, feeling of pain. Each person was asking to be seen.
Rogelio, 21, works overnights at an office. Kicked out of his last residence, he “can’t even afford an apartment.” Last week, he said, he dropped out of college in order to keep up with his car payments. “My problems are smaller than other people’s. But to me, those problems are still big.” A man who doesn’t give his name said that he got hurt on the job only to find out that the state’s workers’ comp system had been gutted. Leah, 17, related that she’s the daughter of an Army veteran of 20 years—then asked, quietly, how we can help veterans with “mental issues, PTSD, after the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.” On and on.
Talarico answered each in turn and, at the end, offered a more expansive response. “I want to be honest that, like many of you, I am tempted by hopelessness,” he said. The candidate, who trained as a seminarian, said that when he feels this way, he often returns to a line in the Gospel of Luke. “Jesus says something really strange. He says, ‘Blessed are you who weep.’ ” How, he asked, can someone who’s weeping be blessed? “In our culture, we tend to avoid grief.”
None of this was off the cuff. It was so well-polished it gleamed. But it was also uncommonly—painfully—earnest, in a way that few politicians would risk. “If your heart is breaking, as you watch what’s happening to our beloved country, it means you still have a heart,” he said. “And I want you to trust that.” In the middle of the crowd, Talarico briefly looked taller, his shoulders wider. His voice sounded deeper. “I want you to protect that. Because that is what’s going to get us out of all of this. Blessed are you who weep.” ★
news.summary: One guy has a decent chance of flipping the state blue. The other guy excels at surviving scandal. Their Senate race shows what the rest of America gets wrong about manliness in Texas.

news.title: Advice for Men From Jennifer Welch, the Profane ‘Mother’ of the Dirtbag Left
news.text:
A few days after Lindsey Graham died, Welch drew listeners’ attention to one of the Republican senator’s last known photographs: Graham holding an upright model of a Ukrainian SkyFall drone interceptor and grinning. “He liked cock, as we all know,” Welch said. “The worst-kept secret in Washington, DC. And he liked killing, you know, the biggest war hawk on the planet. And there he is with a black cock that kills, right before he dies.” There is no way that any political PR person lets their candidate talk to her now, I thought when I heard it. And yet the interviews kept coming.
“I guess that’s the superpower of being a white woman,” says Hasan Piker, who has broadcast with Welch. “I don’t think women of color get the same bandwidth, which I’m sure Jennifer would agree with, and I have a lot more liberties in the way that I speak on issues than women do. I mean, she’s doing it. She’s very good.”
“Don Lemon and Mehdi Hasan say that to me a lot,” Welch says, with no apparent satisfaction, when we meet at a coffee shop in Manhattan. We sit at a sidewalk table, and she keeps her voice down. “They say, ‘You can get away with saying more stuff than we can.’ ”
Welch moved to New York from Oklahoma last year, and she’s still adjusting to the number of I’ve Had It fans around her. One guy made hand-hearts at her through the door of a nail salon. Another came out from behind the wheel of an Amazon delivery truck and expressed his admiration. In Piker’s livestream and subreddit, she is the “leader of the wine mom vanguard” or, simply, “mother.” “They’re like, ‘Oh my God, this white lady’s fighting for us,’ ” she explains. “But it also makes me sad that they don’t see more of us, that I’m novel.”
Welch and her former Bravo costar and now cohost, Angie “Pumps” Sullivan, have been podcasting since 2022. Listeners liked their apolitical rants, their taunts about President Trump (whom they call “Canks,” short for Cankles), and that it all came from two middle-aged blonde women with Southern accents. The podcast gained left-wing political cred over the past two years, as it channeled disillusionment over the defeat of Kamala Harris into criticism of the Democratic Party, including remarkably challenging interviews with Cory Booker and Rahm Emanuel.
“That open-mindedness has made her this iconic figure now with even young men,” Piker says. Today, the podcast has over a million YouTube subscribers and is a Democratic campaign “must-stop,” as a Fox News article put it.
The 2024 presidential election has been called the “testosterone election” (Hulk Hogan’s RNC shirt-ripping, “childless cat ladies,” gender-voting gap), which makes the 2026 midterms a referendum on the testosterone administration. Welch has a very specific take on the role of masculinity in today’s politics, which she touches on in her new book, Not Today, Fascists.
The book lays out, in non-grad-school English, Welch’s case for why today’s Republican-controlled government is Christo-fascist. Drawing from her life as an atheist in the Bible Belt, her close-reading of the news, and her discussions with NYU history professor Ruth Ben-Ghiat, it concludes with a plea for Democrats and their supporters to abandon the corporate-donor model of politics in order to restore democratic credibility and take positions that will improve the lives of the largest number of people. Along the way, she argues that Trump 2’s emphasis on manliness is a feature of its authoritarian leanings. In a chapter on terminology, she writes, “Fascist regimes are led by a strongman, an authoritarian leader marked by displays of hypermasculinity and demands for obedience and loyalty. (Ours happens to wear a full face of orange makeup each and every day.)”
“You have this juxtaposition of ‘We’re such big strong men,’ but meanwhile Trump’s groping a UFC fighter, saying, ‘You’re a good-looking guy,’ ” Welch tells me. (To be fair: It was more of an extended handshake into thigh pat than a grope.) “And listen, I don’t give a shit about that stuff.” LGBTQ+ rights are a through line of Welch’s political commentary, and her new book argues that trans people have been scapegoated by the Republican Party. In her world, “drag queen” is not an insult. (“Failed drag queen,” as she has called JD Vance, definitely is.) “But I’m not a religious hypocrite.”
It’s no longer unusual to see a left-leaning political figure dabble in gay jokes at the expense of Republicans, and it’s bizarrely familiar to those who remember the commentary about 2004 presidential candidate John Kerry’s cheesesteak order. One difference between then and now, says Josh Helfgott, the LGBTQ+ activist behind TikTok’s Gay News, is how the right has shifted rhetorical focus from gay people to trans people, a smaller marginalized group. “Generally what I see Democrats going after, when they tend to critique Republicans, is how they’re performing being a man,” Helfgott says. But “if your punchline is that a man seems feminine and that thus feminine is shameful, you can be perpetuating the same narrative.” Even if liberals talk about closeted conservatives from a position of support for LGBTQ+ rights, he says, “When I hear these things, I think about a gay kid in middle school hearing it. I worry they will see it as another reason why it’s bad to be who they are.”
Still, Welch differs from the archetypal #Resistance-era lib in many ways, one of which is that, when she calls Republicans “DL demon queens,” it doesn’t sound like an off-color joke. It sounds, I tell her, like she truly believes repressed or clandestine homosexuality is rampant in Washington, DC.
“Yeah,” Welch says, nodding. “Not only do I think that, Hunter Biden thinks that. Steve Schmidt, who was John McCain’s campaign adviser, thinks that.” Her belief that politicians who espouse anti-LGBTQ+ views are projecting internal conflict has origins in her Oklahoma upbringing. “The most religious people I knew, the ones that wanted to convert you the most, their families were the most dysfunctional,” she says. “If you look at this brand of Christian nationalism that Republicans are promoting, it’s to mask a lot of problems that they have.”
I ask Welch what she thinks a Democrat man should do if Trump or one of his surrogates calls him “effeminate” (Tim Walz), “transgender” (James Talarico), or “Pinky [sic] Herman” (Jon Ossoff). “Be very aggressive in defending masculinity and defending sexuality,” she says. “Say it with your full chest.”
Welch starts offering up free talking points. “Why are Republican men so obsessed with gay sex? Why are they constantly talking about trans people?” I get the feeling she could keep riffing in this vein for a long time. As long as it takes for civility to come back in style. Or maybe it’ll just be like this forever? “Why does Mike Johnson monitor his son’s use of porn? Why does Josh Hawley look really disturbed when he’s kissing his own wife? Because the call is coming from inside your own house.” ★

news.title: The Patriot Post® · Trump and His Voters
news.text:
A new analysis in the Wall Street Journal offers striking evidence that, for all his problems, President Donald Trump has delivered economic benefits to the voters whose support was the foundation of his victory in 2024.

The Wall Street Journal's headline and story synopsis read: "Americans Without College Degrees Are Having One of the Best Job Markets in Years; Unemployment among younger workers who didn't go to college has rarely been lower in recent decades. It is the opposite story for college grads."

The article was based on work done by a think tank called the Burning Glass Institute. Analysts found that "the unemployment rate for workers ages 22 to 34 who never graduated from college" is at one of its lowest points in the last 20 years. Meanwhile, workers with a bachelor's degree or higher are experiencing greater and greater difficulty getting a good job. "Just as job hunters without degrees are having one of their best runs, those with college educations are having one of their worst," the article said.

In the past, analysts noted, the trends for the two groups, degreed and non-degreed, tended to move in the same direction at the same time. Now, they have diverged, with the non-degreed improving and the degreed encountering problems.

It's not that those with college degrees are suddenly at a huge disadvantage compared to those without. A degree still means something. The Wall Street Journal notes that for those workers between ages 25 and 54 who have a college degree, the unemployment rate averaged 2.7% in the last year. For those with some college but no degree, it was 3.6%, and for those with no college at all, it was 4.7%. So the story is not that having no degree is better than having a degree. The story is that the economic circumstances of non-college-degree workers are improving faster than those with degrees.

Now the politics. A key part of Trump's rise and hold on power has been the support of voters who do not have a college degree. Trump's success has prompted hundreds of stories on the "educational divide" in politics -- how educational status increasingly determines one's politics. The bottom line of all those stories is that voters without degrees support Trump, and voters with degrees support Trump's opponents.

Look at the exit polls from the 2024 election. Among those who never attended college, Trump won with 62% of the vote. Among those who had some college but no degree, Trump won with 51%. Among those who had an associate's degree, Trump won with 57%. Put them all together, and Trump won those without a bachelor's degree with 56% of the vote. And remember -- those without a bachelor's degree made up well over half of the total electorate.

On the other side, then-Vice President Kamala Harris won those with a bachelor's degree with 53% of the vote. Among those who had an advanced degree, Harris won with 59% of the vote.

With Trump, it was a phenomenon that was apparent from the very start of his political career, beginning with the Iowa caucuses in January 2016. "Trump overwhelmingly leads rivals in support from less educated Americans," a headline from PBS reads.

Now, years later, in a second presidential term, the essential storyline is this: Candidate appeals to a group. Candidate wins with that group's support. In office, candidate looks after that group. The cornpone version of it is the phrase, "You got to dance with them what brung you." In this case, Trump got elected on the strength of people without college degrees, and people without college degrees are doing better under his administration.

Of course, it's not that simple. Behind the numbers, there is profound economic and social dislocation. Among the biggest problems is the state of the nation's colleges and universities, many of which offer a product so insanely expensive that it has set off widespread debate on whether a college education is worth it. Still, the belief in college is so ingrained in the American psyche that schools are turning out more graduates than ever, even as AI replaces some of the work they do.

On the other side, people without college degrees, with lower wages, are struggling to pay the same high prices for groceries, gas and other necessities as those with degrees. That has led to Trump's approval rating falling into negative territory with the non-college voters who elected him.

Looking at the details inside a Fox News poll from the summer, the president was underwater with voters who might be expected to be with him. With white voters who do not have a college degree, Trump was at 43% approval, 57% disapproval. That is essentially the opposite result of the 2024 exit polls.

It will also probably mean defeat for Republicans trying to keep control of the House in November's midterm elections. Nevertheless, on one of the most basic measures of economic health -- having a job -- the prospects of those without a college degree are improving under the president they supported. And that has likely created a stable core of support for Trump in what could be a very bumpy second half of his term.

This content originally appeared on the Washington Examiner at www.washingtonexaminer.com/daily-memo/4717301/trump-2024-voters-economic-outlook/.

news.title: The Patriot Post® · SAVE America Act v. Packing Supreme Court: Devil in the Details
news.text:
In February 2026, the U.S. House passed the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility America Act to require proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and an approved form of government photo ID to cast a ballot. 

Every House Republican voted for the SAVE America Act, but every Democrat except one voted against this election integrity measure. 

When the Senate sought to consider the House-passed bill in March 2026, every Republican supported the proposal, and every Democrat opposed it. The unanimous opposition of Democrats prevented the Senate from attaining the 60 votes needed under Senate rules and the bill failed to proceed. 

President Donald Trump and many conservative activists have urged Senate Republicans to invoke a procedural “nuclear option” to change the Senate rules so that the SAVE America Act and all legislation can proceed with a simple majority.

Many Senate Republicans, including several of its most conservative members, oppose lowering the 60-vote threshold. They believe it will damage the institution’s deliberative nature and make it harder to block extreme Democratic legislation when there is a Democratic president with House and Senate majorities.

While many conservatives have vented their frustration against Senate Republicans, Democrats see another villain thwarting their efforts to implement an increasingly liberal agenda: the Republican-appointed majority on the U.S. Supreme Court. 

On Sept. 2, 2026, the House voted on a proposed constitutional amendment to keep nine justices on the U.S. Supreme Court — the number for the past 157 years. The “Keep 9” proposal comes as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is saying “everything is on the table” to deal with a Supreme Court majority that Democrats find objectionable.

Former House Majority Whip James Clyburn, D-S.C, called for adding four justices to the Supreme Court in a recent “Meet the Press” interview. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., have called for adding at least four new seats to the Court. California Gov. Gavin Newson is “warming to the idea.”

The views on court-packing expressed by these current Democratic leaders stand in stark contrast to those of Clinton-appointed Former Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who opposed court-packing. 

In 1983, then-Sen. Joe Biden called President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1937 attempt at court-packing a “bonehead idea” and a “terrible, terrible mistake.” During a presidential primary debate in 2019, Biden said adding more justices to the Supreme Court would destroy “any credibility the Court has at all.”

Conservative opponents of the Democrats’ court-packing scheme argue that Democrats and their liberal activists want a Supreme Court that will view the Constitution as a “living, breathing document” that can be interpreted to impose a far-left agenda on America. 

The next time there is a Democratic president and Democratic majorities in Congress, many conservatives believe they will eliminate the Senate’s 60-vote requirement to enact a wish list of liberal legislation. This list will include a national election law that overrides every photo ID, citizenship verification or clean voter rolls requirement that Republicans have been able to pass at the state or federal level. 

The House vote on the “Keep 9” amendment fell short of the two-thirds needed to advance a constitutional amendment. Consistent with their votes against the SAVE America Act, only one Democrat voted to “Keep 9” while 205 voted against it. 

The independence of the Supreme Court must be preserved from a future Congress and president manipulating its size for political gain. And size does matters: the smaller the size, the less opportunity for stalemates or legislating from the bench.

Republicans and their conservative allies should recognize who their real opponents are and turn their attention to an election that is less than two months away.

And voters should know these details behind the debate to discern differences between the SAVE America Act and packing the Supreme Court before they decide which party should control our Congress come November.

news.title: Luxury Cotswolds hotel loved by celebrities is accused of hosting 'Ibiza-style' parties as neighbours claim loud music, fireworks and helicopters keep them up at night
news.text:
A luxury Cotswolds hotel loved by celebrities has been accused of hosting rowdy parties with neighbours claiming loud music, fireworks and helicopters are keeping them up at night.

The swish Estelle Manor at Eynsham Park near Witney has quickly become a hangout for the stars, with its sprawling grounds, wide range of lavish restaurants, and enormous Roman-themed bath house.

Kim Kardashian even flew in from Los Angeles on her £100million private jet to join Lewis Hamilton for a secret rendezvous in February - the first time they were ever pictured together.

But families living in sleepy North Leigh - which neighbours the members-only hotel - are less impressed, after an alien-themed end-of-summer party allegedly caused disturbance.

Estelle Manor invited its well-heeled clients - who pay £3,750 each year plus a £1,000 joining fee - to its 'otherworldly invasion' event recently, and locals say it was one of many 'Ibiza-style' parties that have kept them up all night.

Some residents have contacted the council and police after claiming their rural idyll was invaded by helicopters flying wealthy revellers into the event, while booming music filled the countryside.

One posted on reviews site Tripadvisor: 'We are not Ibiza! You are repeat offenders with your antisocial, disruptive late night thumping music which you subject us all to.

'Blasting out across the whole area late at night. It is ridiculously loud and we live 1.5 miles away - the volume is unacceptable.

'You are keeping families up, our neighbours, children and agitating pets and wildlife, I can only imagine what poor North Leigh has to put up with, being on your literal doorstep.'

It comes almost exactly a year after locals complained to Oxfordshire County Councillor Liam Walker about a similar loud party at Estelle Manor which kept them awake into the small hours.

In response, he said: 'They have a licence until 1am but I'm told the music shall be winding down at around 12:30am.'

Pictures posted to Estelle Manor's Instagram page show off the end-of-summer party in its full glory with dancers in alien outfits taking to the stage next to the pool, and a spaceship-themed DJ tent in the background.

The caption boasts that guests were 'dancing the night away' during the event.

Estelle Manor lies on a 85-acre estate in the heart of the Cotswolds, long a hotspot for celebrities and potentially the new home of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle.

The Grade-II listed mansion boasts an 'uber-chic' design according to Conde Nast Traveller who ranked it as one of the top places in the UK to relax.

Two padel courts, a large state-of-the-art gym and also 60-acres to explore are all part of a stay at the house. 

A Japanese restaurant by ex-Nobu alumnus Sergej Leonenko is in the pipeline as is a grill restaurant set in the kitchen garden's glasshouse. 

Guests get around the place by either using the pink bikes on site, or by jumping in one of the electric Land Rovers at hand. There is also a helipad in the grounds for anyone arriving by air. 

There are sheep, Shetland ponies, chickens and other farm animals on site. 

A strict no-picture policy allows the utmost privacy for their elite guests, as people are asked to place a sticker over their phone cameras when arriving. 

Estelle Manor is owned by hospitality entrepreneur Sharan Pasricha of Ennismore, whose portfolio also includes the Hoxton hotels, private members' club Maison Estelle in London, and Gleneagles in Perthshire. 

But unlike Gleneagles, it's been created from scratch under the guidance of Sharan and his wife Eiesha, a successful businesswoman and daughter of Indian billionaire Sunil Mittal.

High-profile guests have also included Kate Moss, Princess Beatrice and Kamala Harris, although there is no suggestion any of these celebrities attended any of the disruptive events. 

Hamilton and Kardashian sent shockwaves across the globe when they were spotted checking into the lavish UK hotel and members only club earlier this year. 

It marked the first time the rumoured couple was pictured together following reports that they were embroiled in a 'secret romance'.

It was said that the SKIMs mogul and the Formula 1 ace enjoyed an intimate dinner and a couple's massage as part of their romantic weekend getaway at the glamorous hotel.

Billionaire heiress Eve Jobs and Team GB Olympic gold medallist Harry Charles tied the knot at Estelle Manor last summer, with Elton John hosting a special set.

The Daily Mail has approached Estelle Manor for comment.

news.title: Texas Latinos Are Turning Against Republican Party
news.text: Latino voters in three competitive Texas House districts favor Democrats by 56 percent to 36 percent, according to a new Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision poll. That movement could affect control of Congress as closely divided battlegrounds can be decided by relatively small changes among major voting blocs. Republicans entered the 2026 cycle hoping President Donald Trump's improved showing with Latino voters in 2024 represented a lasting political realignment. However, the new figures suggest that support was conditional, with economic frustration and opposition to the administration's immigration enforcement giving Democrats an opening. Democratic and Republican candidates in districts along the Mexico border, suburban Fort Worth and the Austin-San Antonio corridor face a substantially changed electoral landscape. Democrats Are Building a Texas Lead Hart Research conducted the 2026 Latino Battleground survey for TelevisaUnivision from August 6 to 17 among 1,500 Latino registered voters in 17 competitive congressional districts. The Texas sample comprised 300 interviews in the 23rd, 28th and 35th districts. The reported margin of sampling error for the full survey was plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Among Latino respondents in the three Texas districts, the self-reported 2024 presidential vote was tied at 44 percent each for Trump and then-Vice President Kamala Harris. When asked about the 2026 congressional ballot, however, 56 percent supported Democratic candidates and 36 percent backed Republicans. "Latino voters aren't locked into one party," Kate Coleman, a senior vice president at TelevisaUnivision, told Axios. "They're paying close attention and making decisions based on who shows up for them, and how they're showing up." The Texas sample covered three House contests. In the 23rd Congressional District, Republican Brandon Herrera, Democrat Katy Padilla Stout and independent Ben Mendoza are running for an open seat. Democratic incumbent Henry Cuellar hopes to hold the seat in the 28th District against challenges from Republican Tano Tijerina and Green Party candidate Marlon Duran. And in the 35th District, Democrat Johnny Garcia and Republican Carlos De La Cruz are vying to replace Democratic Representative Greg Casar. A Larger Battleground Movement Across the 17 competitive House districts surveyed, Democrats led Republicans by 58 percent to 35 percent among Latino registered voters on the generic congressional ballot. That 23-point margin was twice the 11-point advantage Harris held over Trump in the same respondents' self-reported 2024 vote. Among California respondents in the battleground survey, 57 percent favored Democratic congressional candidates and 33 percent backed Republicans. Latino respondents in two Florida swing districts moved from a 1-point Trump advantage in their self-reported 2024 vote to a 13-point Democratic lead on the 2026 ballot. The survey also found that 11 percent of Latino respondents who said they backed Trump in 2024 now support Democratic congressional candidates. The findings do not establish how individual districts will vote. Generic-ballot preferences can change before Election Day, while turnout, candidate quality and local issues will shape each contest separately. Prices and Immigration Drive Voter Discontent Economic pressure appears to be the clearest source of Republican vulnerability. Sixty-five percent of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of prices and the cost of living. When asked which party they trusted more to lower prices, 62 percent chose Democrats in Congress and 36 percent selected Republicans. Immigration enforcement presents another problem. Sixty-two percent disapproved of the administration's approach to enforcement and deportations, while 64 percent gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement an unfavorable rating. Among Latino independents, 65 percent gave ICE an unfavorable rating. Those results do not amount to a wholesale rejection of border enforcement. They indicate dissatisfaction with how the administration has implemented its policies, alongside concern about household costs. Overall, 63 percent disapproved of Trump's job performance and 36 percent approved. National Polling Shows Broader Latino Discontent A national Pew Research Center survey provided an earlier indication of Latino dissatisfaction with the administration. Conducted in English and Spanish from October 6 to 16, 2025, the poll found that 70 percent of Latino adults disapproved of Trump's job performance and 65 percent disapproved of his administration's handling of immigration. The Latino sample comprised 4,923 adults, with a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points at the 95 percent confidence level. Pew used a combination of online and live telephone interviews, with results weighted to national population benchmarks. Its scope differed substantially from the new Hart Research poll. Pew surveyed a nationally representative sample of Latino adults, while Hart surveyed Latino registered voters in 17 competitive House districts. The two polls therefore show a similar direction of opinion but measure different populations. Meanwhile, a May UnidosUS poll, which surveyed 3,000 Latino registered voters nationally and across 32 competitive congressional districts, with a margin of error of plus or minus 1.8 percentage points, found that 54 percent said they would support a Democratic House candidate in the 2026 election, matching the Democratic share of the Latino vote in CBS News' 2024 House exit polling. In the UnidosUS poll, conducted by BSP Research and Shaw & Company Research from April 27 to May 14, 27 percent said they would support a Republican candidate, while 19 percent were undecided. What Happens Next With the midterm campaign in its final stretch, Republicans must determine whether their 2024 support can be recovered. Democrats, meanwhile, still need to convert favorable battleground polling into turnout on November 3. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Shakeema Edwards.
news.summary: Latino voters shift toward Democrats in Texas battlegrounds amid discontent over high prices, immigration and Trump's presidency.

news.title: Everyone wants to win working-class voters. But have they realized many are women?
news.text:
This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th. Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

Congressional candidate JoAnna Mendoza can quickly rattle off prices from the grocery store in the small town of Eloy, Arizona, where she grew up. A couple of months ago, a pound of ground beef was going for about $13, a tomato was $1.50 and “a freaking cucumber was like $3.” 

She knows because she’s a single mom to a 10-year-old, and she’s struggled with the same things most working women are facing: finding a steady job, a good pediatrician and childcare that isn’t going to break the bank. Mendoza’s parents were farmworkers, and she spent 20 years in the military because there were few economic opportunities for her back home. Now she’s running for a seat in the U.S. House to represent Arizona’s 6th congressional district. 

Working class people, and especially women, like Mendoza, have rarely had a seat at the political table, though they make up nearly half of working-class voters, the group Republicans desperately want to cling onto and that Democrats hope to draw back.

It’s a group that is more diverse now than it’s ever been. Gone are the days when the only image of a working-class voter was a blue-collar White man who works in a factory and drives a truck, though that is still who politicians often pander to. 

Political messaging that speaks to the everyday needs of the diversifying working class could recapture the interest of the group, which has long been disillusioned by political candidates who don’t actually understand them.

Definitions of what makes a working-class voter differ depending on who you ask. If it’s education — those who have less than a bachelor’s degree — then nearly half of the working class is women; in parts of the country, most of them are also people of color, said Valerie Wilson, a labor economist at the Economic Policy Institute who has studied working-class people. If working-class voters are those working low-wage jobs, then they are already majority women, who occupy two-thirds of the 40 lowest-paid occupations. 

“The sort of traditional view of ‘working class’ was a White man in a hard hat, a construction worker, maybe someone who was in manufacturing,” Wilson said. That’s gone now as those jobs have disappeared and service-sector jobs dominated by women have become the primary field for people without college degrees. Working-class people are now mostly service, retail and care workers, a group often forgotten in political and economic conversations in part because the work has been seen as gendered labor, though they have a front seat to most of the financial troubles that have plagued the country over the past several years. You don’t have to tell women, who do the majority of consumer purchases in this country, that groceries and gas are more expensive. They’ve lived it. 

A fundamental misunderstanding of working-class voters — and the messages that resonate with them — caused Democrats to fumble their advantage with this group in recent years. Twenty years ago, Democrats enjoyed a 14-point advantage with voters who didn’t have a bachelor’s degree. By 2024, Republicans had a 6-point advantage instead. In the 2024 presidential election, working-class voters favored President Donald Trump by 14 points. 

Republicans have effectively understood that their voters want good, secure jobs that allow them to live independently and support their family. Working-class voters respect people who talk to them directly — Trump’s “straight talk” — and those who have been successful through their own hard work, social inequality expert Joan C. Williams argued in 2016. 

“What they want is what my father-in-law had: steady, stable, full-time jobs that deliver a solid middle-class life to the 75% of Americans who don’t have a college degree. Trump promises that,” Williams wrote after Trump was elected in 2016. “I doubt he’ll deliver, but at least he understands what they need.”

A decade later, Trump indeed has not delivered on many of his economic promises. His second term has been dominated by war in Iran and aggressive tariff policies that have driven up prices rather than balanced trade, as he promised. That has eroded Trump’s advantage with his strongest working class supporters, White people, who now disapprove of his handling of the economy.

Democrats see an opening this midterm cycle. A recent poll found that adults who self-describe as working class expect progressive Democrats to best represent their interests, followed by moderate Republicans. Working-class women already tend to skew more progressive than men: Every racial subgroup of working-class women, except White women, favored Kamala Harris over Trump in 2024. 

This year, Democrats, more than Republicans, have put up women working-class candidates who have both a personal background and message that could connect with voters. It’s something of a litmus test for the Democratic Party: Can working-class women candidates help them win back working-class votes? 

For her part, Mendoza said she’s not a fan of the Democrats’ messaging. 

“Can Democrats just be normal and not have to use $50 words to talk to people?” Mendoza said. “Spending 20 years in the military, retiring from the Marine Corps, I personally drop about 20 to 30 f-bombs a day,” she said. “Sometimes you gotta throw an f-bomb.”

She approaches conversations with voters the way she talks to the moms of the children on her son’s little league baseball team. They’re worried about the cost of child care, which is so expensive that it doesn’t even make sense to get back into the workforce even though they could use the extra income. They’re worried about school supplies and utility bills, just like Mendoza, who spent more than $100 on her son’s supplies this summer and $391 on her most recent electric bill. 

“The majority of women are what I like to call the chief financial officers of their families, and they’re sitting here trying to figure out how they’re going to make ends meet,” Mendoza said. 

Williams argued in her book “Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back” that Democrats have focused too much on college-educated liberals and forgotten about working-class people. The messages became about policies that would help people advance in their jobs instead of policies that supported people who worked hard and just wanted to earn a living.

For working-class voters, including women, class can trump gender as the determining factor behind a vote. Look at the 2016 presidential race: White working-class women voted for Trump over Hillary Clinton by a 27-point margin. 

“Working-class women are working-class people, something upper-middle-class women often forget,” Williams said. Their preferred candidate: another working-class person. 

If Democrats pay attention, future cycles may have more candidates like Kaela Berg, a flight attendant and single mom who ran for a highly contested seat representing Minnesota’s 2nd congressional district in the U.S. House. Before she lost her primary in August, she was running her campaign between flights, talking about living paycheck to paycheck, going without health insurance during the pandemic and at one point living in a friend’s basement. She never graduated college and has long been active in her union. 

“I don’t have to look at a white paper on affordability. I know people are struggling and that this economy is hurting people,” Berg told The 19th. 

Polling by Emily’s List, which works to elect Democratic women who support abortion rights, has found that women are more likely than men to be struggling financially, more likely to say they are looking for candidates who will fight for them and also more likely to blame Washington for their financial struggles. 

“It was very clear based on that research that driving wins in this environment, in this economy, was really going to hinge on putting leaders in front of voters who truly get it, truly understand their struggles. And the reason for that is because the depth and breadth of people’s financial struggle is really stark,” said Jessica Mackler, the president of Emily’s List. 

The past couple of years have been particularly challenging for working-class women in the economy. They returned to work in high numbers after the pandemic, benefiting from a climate in which businesses were offering better benefits, more flexibility and higher pay, which allowed them to move into good jobs. But those improvements were short-lived.

“We’re seeing a pretty stunning reversal of that that is impacting the real working-class jobs that are sort of manual labor, low-wage, low-education requirement jobs predominantly held by women,” said Kate Bahn, the chief economist and senior vice president of research at the Institute for Women’s Policy Research, a think tank focused on gender and economic equity.

The evidence is in the gender pay gap: After years of shrinking, the gap actually widened over the past two years for the first time since the 1960s. 

Working class women are facing a labor market far more unstable than in the last election cycle, and they’re looking for candidates who understand that, voters told The 19th.

Jenny Cook, a paraprofessional who works with special needs children in Oakdale, Minnesota, has been knocking on doors with her union this summer in support of candidates like Peggy Flanagan, who is running to represent Minnesota in the Senate and often talks about growing up in Section 8 housing with a single mother who relied on food stamps. 

When she thinks of the candidates who have stuck out, Cook thinks of people like Omar Fateh, who ran for mayor in Minneapolis last year. The fact that he was a renter stayed with her. “That feels like someone who has a lived experience that mirrors mine and many others in a way that I don’t know that every politician can really wrap their heads around what that’s like,” she said. 

For her, it’s not just about someone who understands that rents are high or that groceries are expensive, but about a candidate who understands how destabilizing all those things can be.

Cook often lives paycheck to paycheck and sells plasma or items on Facebook Marketplace to keep up with bills. She offers her own example: Last winter, one of her students had a bed bug situation at home. To try to avoid bringing it home with her after work, she’d toss all her clothes immediately into the dryer so the heat could kill any eggs that may have hitchhiked on her. But, because her dryer was old, the belt broke and she couldn’t afford a new one. So, in the middle of Minnesota winter, she started taking her clothes off in the entryway and throwing them on the front step. On weekends, she’d carry them to the laundromat. 

“The amount of sleep I lost, and I just like, I feel like I’m still trying to recover from the financial impact of just that,” Cook said. “I always feel like one crisis away from everything falling apart.”

When she’s out doorknocking, she hears disillusionment. She hears exhaustion. So many people are so stuck in the struggle of day-to-day survival that they can barely plug into politics at all. Few candidates break through the noise. 

“It almost feels like, ‘Wouldn’t it be nice if I could pay attention to who my candidates are and care on that deep of a level?’” Cook said. 

Roxy Hoda, a hospitality worker at Target Field in Minnesota, says affordability is her No. 1 issue. The healthcare costs for her family of four tripled in the past two years. She’s paying $2,100 a month for health insurance with an $8,000 deductible that she already blew through at the start of the year when her 4-year-old son was hospitalized with asthma. 

She is also supporting Flanagan, whom she called “a breath of fresh air.” 

“As a woman of color that has come from that similar background as me, I know that she understands what it is to be a woman of color in this society,” Hoda said. 

It’s the one bright spot that has helped assuage some of her disillusionment with a Democratic Party that she feels has “been too scared to really get emotional.” 

For Hoda, it comes down to this: “We just need to know that you understand and you relate, and you’re with us and you’re fighting.”
news.summary: The working class isn't just White men in hard hats anymore. Women candidates may be the ones who can earn votes
