news.title: Cuellar and Tijerina spar over who delivers for a South Texas district redrawn to favor the GOP
news.text:
WASHINGTON — While Congress was on break this August, Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, popped up at over 60 events in his district, many of them to announce funding for local projects he secured from his longtime perch on the House Appropriations Committee.

Cuellar has used this time-tested style of retail politicking throughout his nearly 22 years in Congress, making himself a fixture at ribbon cuttings, high school graduation ceremonies and other community events across his South Texas district. Staring down another competitive race this fall, the “King of Laredo,” as he’s known to some constituents, is back at it touting dollars brought home for Title I public schools, health clinics and water line improvements.

“I don’t wait til election year,” he said in an interview. “I’m out there month after month throughout the year — election year [and] non-election year, we’re going out there. I always say I’m a member of Congress, but I run as a mayor. And by that I mean, I look at what are the issues that affect people locally.”

His Republican challenger, Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina, says Cuellar’s crown is slipping.

Tijerina, who has served as the county executive since 2015, is a former Democrat who joined the GOP shortly after the 2024 election. On the campaign trail, the two have sparred over who gets to take credit for federal dollars brought back to the district. And Tijerina says Cuellar’s record does not match his reputation for delivering the goods.

“In Webb County, we’re $1.5 billion behind on infrastructure,” Tijerina said. “If he is the kind of man that brings in the money, why doesn’t he bring in the $1.5 billion of infrastructure?”

These are the hyper-local concerns both men are running on in a race with national implications, both for control of the U.S. House and insights into one of the most politically fluid regions of the country. Texas’ 28th Congressional District, which has an eligible voting population that is nearly 87 percent Hispanic, runs along the border from Maverick County to McAllen, covering a historically Democratic area that has swung rapidly to the right in recent years.

The 28th District, under its latest boundaries, voted for Trump by a 10-point margin in 2024 while being functionally tied in the U.S. Senate race. Joe Biden won it by 9 percentage points in 2020 and Beto O’Rourke carried the district by a 32-point margin in 2018. 

Republicans redrew the district last year to be slightly more Trump-leaning. But under the old lines, even while running under the cloud of an indictment for bribery and money laundering charges, Cuellar outran Trump, winning by nearly 6 percentage points even as Trump carried the district by a 7-point margin.

This year, the race between Cuellar and Tijerina will be a test of how much crossover appeal each man can generate — Cuellar to the district’s Trump voters, and Tijerina to voters who, even if they cast their ballot for Trump, have stayed loyal to Cuellar. 

Both are pitching their case to members of the opposite party — in a region where a critical chunk of voters have not shown strong adherence to either the Democratic or Republican label. 

Cuellar, arguably the most conservative Democrat in the U.S. House, can point to his seniority, earmarking skills and public break with Democrats on border policy during the Biden era. Tijerina, as a former Democrat himself, has an in with fellow party switchers, and has emphasized his record cutting tax rates as Webb County judge. He has also criticized Cuellar over the incumbent’s bribery indictment. Cuellar, who denied wrongdoing, was cleared of the charges when he received a pardon from Trump late last year.

A recent poll from Texas Southern University found Cuellar was making inroads in his crossover appeals, winning nearly a quarter of likely midterm voters who backed Trump in 2024. That fueled Cuellar’s 45% to 34% lead in the poll, which showed him with a bigger lead and more Trump support than the Democratic candidates in neighboring South Texas districts.

It would not be the first time Cuellar has successfully capitalized on his crossover support to win. He routinely runs ahead of Democratic statewide candidates in the district, a history he attributes to his willingness to break from the party on the border in particular, along with his support for the oil and gas industry that employs thousands of his constituents. Cuellar won Webb County in 2024, for example, by about 21 percentage points, while Trump narrowly carried it. In neighboring Starr County, Cuellar outran Kamala Harris by over 27 percentage points.

He also believes Republicans unwittingly helped him out when they redrew his district, one of five Democratic seats targeted in the GOP’s mid-decade redistricting last summer. In moving the 28th District deeper into the Rio Grande Valley, Republican mapmakers increased the percentage that went to Trump in 2024. But the unusual amount of ticket-splitting in South Texas meant that the percentage of voters in the new district who voted for a House Democrat also increased, Cuellar said.

And the district became more Latino, with its eligible voting population jumping from about 69% Hispanic to 87% — meaning a leftward swing in the Latino vote would have a heavier impact on the seat.

Cuellar emphasized that he was not taking anything for granted, but he expressed confidence in his ability to win over former Trump voters.

“We’ve had that historically, and we’ll get that again,” he said.

But Tijerina said he hears from voters of all political stripes that are ready to move on from Cuellar in the wake of his indictment saga. He believes he can make inroads among Cuellar’s Democratic base especially over the alleged corruption.

Tijerina is also considered a much stronger opponent than Cuellar’s 2024 challenger, a white veteran who had never held office before and who struggled to raise the money needed for a competitive run.

With Cuellar up against a fellow elected official this time, Tijerina said the race will turn on local issues rather than national ones — a claim he says is backed up by his campaign’s polling.

“It’s not about Republican, it’s not about Democrat. It’s about doing the right thing, especially when we have a record to run on,” Tijerina said. “That’s what people are seeing, and I think that’s what’s being exposed right now.”

The fight to claim credit

Cuellar has sought to tie Tijerina to a handful of key issues that he believes have caused Trump voters in the district to turn on the GOP — tariffs among them.

The Port of Laredo does the most land-based trade in the country, accounting for 40% of all U.S.-Mexico commerce exchange, making tariff policy and ongoing negotiations over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement more important in this district than nearly any other in the country.

When asked about Trump’s tariff policy, Tijerina said the president “is doing an incredible job” attempting to rebalance the country’s trade deficit. He argued that, as important as U.S.-Mexico trade is in the district, voters will realize that changes to the tariff rate will benefit them in the long run.

“The tariff situation needs to be balanced,” Tijerina said. “And I think once it becomes balanced, people will be making more. The capitalism will happen even stronger and better, and people will be making more money.”

Trump last year set a 10% tariff on potash from Mexico and 25% for products not covered by the countries’ existing trade deal, though the policy was overturned earlier this year by the U.S. Supreme Court. The president then used other authorities to issue a new tariff on non-covered products from Mexico. 

Cuellar said Trump’s tariffs have hurt the district and provided him with an opening to engage with the president’s voters. Support for the trade war, he said, is a nonstarter, referencing Tijerina’s 2025 comments supporting the president’s increase in tariff rates.

“You don’t say that in Laredo, the largest port of entry in the country,” Cuellar said. “That’s not good.”

The two have also gone back and forth over data centers, an issue of much debate in the city of Laredo. There are no operating or proposed data centers in the city limits, but a 50,000-acre project called “Data City” has been discussed nearby in Webb County.

Tijerina touted his commitment to a ratepayer protection pledge to keep households and businesses from absorbing the energy costs created by data centers, and he said the facilities should be generating their own water and electricity. But he also emphasized that the U.S. needs to beat China in the artificial intelligence race.

As Webb County judge, Tijerina said he hasn’t been approached about any data centers — but noted that if AI companies are pursuing data centers on “private property, that’s their prerogative.” And he said data center companies should do more to educate communities about their value.

“I think this will all get resolved,” Tijerina said. “Once upon a time, when you had the windmills and the farms and solar panels, everybody was up in arms about that too for awhile. And then they realize, hey, it’s not as bad as maybe China is pushing this [opposition].”

Cuellar, meanwhile, filed a bill in August entitled the “Ratepayer Bill of Rights Act”, which would require data center companies to disclose their projected and actual electricity and water usage and pay all project-driven costs. Independent assessments would also have to confirm that sufficient water remains for households and businesses during a drought — a subject that Cuellar believes is especially top of mind for voters after the district’s efforts to conduct long-term water planning.

“Data centers [are] going to be a big issue in my district, especially in the Laredo area, because we are looking for secondary sources of water,” Cuellar said.

Both candidates believe they can make hay of one another’s records.

In Tijerina’s first campaign ad, he said he delivered an expansion of the Meals on Wheels program for seniors in Webb County and the delivery of $20 million in utility assistance. But Cuellar says the money for those programs came from federal grants that he secured on the Appropriations Committee or through federal programs he voted for, including Meals on Wheels and the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program.

“We vote on that on appropriations every year,” Cuellar said. “It’s interesting that my opponent[‘s] ads are on programs that are brought in by the federal government and by members of the Appropriations [Committee].”

Tijerina said the credit goes to the cities and counties that apply for the grant funding — and that the earmarks that Cuellar does secure take too long to materialize. Plus, Tijerina said, there are plenty of districts that lack senior appropriators but still get earmarked funds. 

“The number one thing that I”m hearing the most is how neglected our district has been — hearing it from the ground and hearing it from all these elected officials and the people,” Tijerina said. “Henry goes around and parades himself as a money man and as the appropriations committee guy, and unfortunately, I think he has failed all of us all in that aspect.”

In his tenure leading county government, Tijerina said, Cuellar has “never even stepped into my office in 12 years and asked me how and what can he help me with.”

If he does win a seat in Congress, Tijerina said he would lobby for a perch on the Appropriations Committee and work to “bring real money into my district.”

Cuellar is currently the top Democrat on the appropriations subcommittee that oversees funding for the Department of Homeland Security. If he wins and Democrats take the House, he will sit atop the panel that sets the budget for agencies including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

“I’m going to try to bring balance to this issue when it comes to ICE,” Cuellar said. “ICE should be focusing on criminals — not on families, Dreamers, construction workers.”
news.summary: Rep. Henry Cuellar and Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina are both courting crossover support in a region where voters have been willing to defy Democratic or Republican labels.
news.author: Gabby Birenbaum

news.title: AIPAC, Netanyahu and Israel take center stage in New Hampshire Democratic primaries
news.text: One night of primaries in New Hampshire offered Democrats two nearly opposite pictures of their changing relationship with Israel. In the more important race, the Senate primary, Chris Pappas, a moderate congressman with a clear pro-Israel record, defeated a progressive challenger who made Israel and allegations of genocide a central part of her campaign. Hours later, in the race for the House seat Pappas himself is vacating, Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of one of the state’s most powerful political families, cruised to victory after making an anti-AIPAC campaign one of her most prominent weapons. Pappas, 46, quickly won the Democratic Senate primary with about 63% of the vote, securing a place in one of the most important races of the November midterms. He will face Republican John Sununu, a former senator and the son and brother of two former governors, in a contest that could prove significant in the fight for control of the Senate. Democrats must hold the seat of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen — Stefany's mother — and Republicans have already identified New Hampshire as one of their best opportunities. But Pappas is not just another moderate Democrat with a long résumé. If he wins in November, he will be the first openly gay man to serve in the U.S. Senate. He also comes from a family that holds another, far less stately American distinction: His grandfather, Charlie Pappas, is credited with inventing the chicken tender in 1974, the fried chicken strip that has since become a national institution. The Pappas family still owns the Puritan Backroom restaurant, a pilgrimage site for politicians visiting New Hampshire, where Pappas also celebrated his victory. The claim that the family invented the tender is difficult to prove, but Manchester, New Hampshire, has already officially declared itself the “Chicken Tender Capital of the World.” His connection to the Shaheen family also completes an almost perfect political circle. In 1996, when he was a 16-year-old high school student, Pappas volunteered on Jeanne Shaheen’s first campaign for governor. Since then, he has passed through nearly every possible stage of local politics, from the state Legislature to a powerful executive council, before being elected to Congress in 2018. Now, 30 years after handing out campaign literature for her, he is the candidate seeking to replace her in the Senate. For Jerusalem, Pappas has long been considered part of the more Israel-friendly wing of the Democratic Party. AIPAC supported him in previous House races and he was among the Democrats who voted to condemn Palestinian American Rep. Rashida Tlaib over her use of the phrase “from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free.” He supports Israel’s right to defend itself and a two-state solution. But the current primary highlighted just how much the atmosphere inside the party has changed. In recent months, Pappas has distanced himself from Israel’s right-wing government, saying Netanyahu “has to go” and is not a reliable U.S. partner. He also voted present on a proposal to completely eliminate $3.3 billion in aid to Israel and pledged that in the Senate he would support restrictions on shipments of heavy bombs and certain military equipment. That was not enough for his opponent, Dr. Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist and member of the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, the faction that has produced figures such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Manzur accused Israel of “genocide” and claimed Netanyahu controls nearly 90% of Congress and the White House. She called Pappas “AIPAC’s emissary” and accused him of “getting paid” by the lobby in exchange for his votes. Billboards attacking his ties to AIPAC were even put up in his hometown. Manzur managed to narrow the polling gap in recent weeks and ride the same anti-establishment wave that has carried other progressive candidates this year. But on Election Day, it became clear that the establishment is still alive. Pappas had the backing of Kamala Harris, Elizabeth Warren and Mark Kelly and, above all, a nearly absurd financial advantage: He had raised more than $15 million through the end of August, compared with less than $500,000 for Manzur. 'Choose a fighter, not a family name' That same night, however, a few miles away, the family name was working in an entirely different direction. Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of the retiring senator, was on her way to a narrow primary victory for the House seat Pappas is leaving behind. Her main rival, Maura Sullivan, a former Marine officer who served in Iraq and a former senior Obama administration official, tried to turn the political dynasty into a liability. In a campaign ad, she urged voters to “choose a fighter, not a fancy family name” and accused Shaheen of feeling entitled to the seat. Sullivan had already tried to win the same seat in 2018, when Pappas was the one who defeated her in the primary. The “nepo baby” label attached to Shaheen Jr. also has a numerical basis. Nearly $740,000 raised by her campaign came from donors who had previously contributed to her mother. At least one major donor said the senator herself contacted him and asked him to support her daughter. Her father, Billy Shaheen, is also a longtime Democratic establishment figure in New Hampshire who has managed local campaigns for presidential candidates including Jimmy Carter, Al Gore and John Kerry over the years. But Stefany Shaheen has a story of her own. She served on the Portsmouth City Council and chaired its police commission, founded a digital health company and has spent years working on diabetes issues after her eldest daughter was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at age 8 and nearly died. She is the mother of four, is a graduate of programs at MIT and Harvard and wrote a bestselling book about her family’s experience with the disease. Her campaign focused on health care and support for universal health insurance, but in recent weeks Israel and AIPAC took on a more prominent role. Shaheen repeatedly attacked Sullivan over donations from people who had also contributed to AIPAC and aired an ad portraying her as “funded” by the pro-Israel lobby “aligned with Netanyahu.” Her campaign showed an image of Netanyahu alongside the declaration: “Let’s show them New Hampshire’s not for sale.” Sullivan, for her part, insisted that AIPAC itself had neither donated to nor supported her. Shaheen sought to fend off accusations of antisemitism by securing the support of J Street, the liberal pro-Israel lobby considered an ideological rival of AIPAC, as well as pointing to her Jewish supporters. She is a staunch supporter of ending U.S. military aid to Israel and pledged to vote for any proposal to do so. She still describes Israel as an “our strongest ally in the Middle East,” recognizes its right to exist alongside a two-state solution, but on aid and the pro-Israel lobby she is clearly to the left of Democrats of her mother’s generation. Thus, while Pappas demonstrated that a Democrat with a pro-Israel record can still easily defeat a rival who built a significant part of her campaign around attacks on Israel and AIPAC, in the neighboring race the daughter of the senator he is seeking to replace found that one way to prove to voters that she is more than just “the daughter of” is to attack AIPAC and oppose military aid to Israel. The two results do not tell the same story, but they once again demonstrate where the Democratic Party stands in 2026: Israel is no longer a foreign policy issue that candidates can skip over in a primary. It has become a political test in which candidates are expected to choose a clear side.
news.summary: New Hampshire primary night highlights Democrats’ shifting views on Israel: Chris Pappas wins Senate primary despite progressive challenger’s attacks; Stefany Shaheen wins House seat after targeting AIPAC and opposing military aid to Israel
news.author: Daniel Edelson, New York

news.title: Democrats Keep Looking for the “Next Obama.” They Should Do This Instead.
news.text:
The first time I remember hearing Barack Obama’s name was in late 2006 or early 2007. I was sitting in seventh grade social studies, where we were encouraged to discuss current events. “I think he’s going to run for president,” our teacher confided in a knowing yet slightly hushed tone, almost like she still couldn’t quite believe it.

Back then, much of the excitement was bound up in the prospect of America having its first Black president, but Obama ultimately proved himself to be worthy of it. Two decades on, the energy he created has morphed into something decidedly more desperate. Obama is the only Democratic president this century to win reelection and remains one of the country’s most popular political figures. Which might explain why Democrats, looking ahead to congressional elections this fall and a 2028 presidential race whose stakes feel existential, keep looking for the former president’s spiritual successor: someone who can inspire, speak, and above all win, just like the real thing. All summer, voters, consultants, and pundits have repeatedly attached Obama’s name like a Homeric epithet to a bumper crop of young, talented, and mostly male candidates running across the country.

It’s happened to Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, whose self-confident swagger and immigrant-family story have invited the comparison. “It reminded me a lot of the Barack Obama bio,” Jon Favreau, Obama’s former speechwriter, recalled after seeing El-Sayed at a fundraiser.

Then there’s James Talarico, the Texas state representative running for U.S. Senate whose winning primary campaign former New York Times columnist Charles Blow likened to Obama’s 2008 faceoff against Hillary Clinton. After Talarico’s campaign posted footage of the former president stumping with him at a taco shop this spring, the equivalencies flowed in. “I think you have what it takes to be the next Obama and Lord knows we need it!” one Facebook commenter wrote.

The Obama parallel has similarly been lavished on two Democratic governors who look set to cruise to reelection this fall: Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, and Wes Moore of Maryland, who started fielding Obama analogies even before he became the state’s first Black governor. Pete Buttigieg, the former Biden transportation secretary who isn’t officially running for anything right now, has been getting the comparison for years.

Even Graham Platner, the scruffy Maine oyster farmer, was winning Obama-esque praise before his Senate candidacy imploded. Jim Messina, Obama’s 2012 campaign manager, dubbed Platner’s victory speech on primary night a “masterclass” that recalled the 44th president. (A few weeks later, after an ex-girlfriend accused Platner of rape, Messina suggested Platner should “go jump in a Maine lake.”) Further south, Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat who is up for reelection this fall, has been likened to the former president for viral speeches that are already earning him national attention and fueling 2028 chatter.

The search for an Obama inheritor isn’t totally new. Ahead of the 2020 election, Joe Biden, Kamala Harris, and Cory Booker tussled over the former president’s legacy in what the Los Angeles Times perceptively dubbed “the Obama primary.” The search has taken on new proportions and greater urgency as Democrats once again seek to claw their way back to power after yet another Trump presidency. The question is: Even if they find their guy, is an Obama 2.0 what the party needs, now, or in 2028?

To give Democrats their due, trying to re-create a popular two-term commander in chief in the aggregate doesn’t seem like the worst strategy in the world. After the Biden interregnum and Donald Trump’s return, nostalgia for better political times appears broadly felt: A January poll of a hypothetical 2028 third-term matchup against Trump found Obama ahead by double digits. (Neither man can legally be elected again.) Historical patterns are worth taking seriously, too. Every couple of decades, it seems, Democrats turn to a sunny, novel-seeming, relatively young man to resuscitate their party’s political fortunes. It happened with John F. Kennedy in 1960, Jimmy Carter in 1976, and Bill Clinton in 1992. And as Obama proved, lesser-known lawmakers with funny names can sometimes go on to make history.

But there are a few reasons to wonder whether Democrats’ search for “the next Obama” has gotten a little out of hand—and might inadvertently lead the party even deeper into the political wilderness. For one thing, the comparison has become so common that it’s started to lose meaning, and power. The last few years of American politics are littered with Democrats hailed as the next Obama who ended up falling short. The late PBS anchor Gwen Ifill canonized Kamala Harris as “the female Barack Obama” back in 2009, but Harris’ two presidential campaigns both failed. A 2018 New Yorker article about the presidential prospects of Deval Patrick, the former Massachusetts governor, pronounced him “a kind of political heir to Barack Obama” and quoted former Obama advisers favorably comparing the two men. When Patrick did finally launch a 2020 campaign, it lasted just three months.

Obama, of course, isn’t a ghost, and he has been talking up some of the same candidates others are likening to him. Obama called up El-Sayed last month and has publicly praised Talarico, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and other promising young Democrats. Still, not even Obama’s Obamadar is perfect. In 2018, as Beto O’Rourke was weighing a national campaign, the former president was the one drawing comparisons between them. “The reason I was able to make a connection with a sizable portion of the country was because people had a sense that I said what I meant,” Obama said then, making clear that he felt O’Rourke shared that special touch. Former Obama aides reportedly called O’Rourke’s people to offer their help, remarking that the lanky Texan reminded them of their former boss. “He’s Barack Obama, but white,” one Democratic bundler told Politico. Judging by polling and fundraising, though, the rest of the country didn’t agree: O’Rourke ended up dropping out before a single primary vote was cast. That doesn’t mean Obama was wrong about their similarities. But it does suggest that giving party apparatchiks shivers of recognition isn’t enough.

Another factor complicating things for the latest Obama mini-mes: Candidates themselves are starting to lean into the comparison. For them, giving off Obama vibes can be a convenient shortcut to national prominence, campaign contributions, and glowing press. But for the rest of us, it can be hard to tell whether someone is truly an Obama-caliber candidate or is just staring in the mirror a little too hard.

El-Sayed, for example, used to shy away from the parallel. “There are a lot of things I disagree with President Obama on—in terms of both domestic and, certainly, international politics,” he told Vox during his 2018 run for Michigan governor. “I’m not him, and I have no intention of being him.” Last month, though, he struck a different tone. “I never saw myself in politics until I saw him give that 2004 speech on the DNC floor,” El-Sayed admiringly declared of the keynote address that propelled Obama to national stardom. El-Sayed has since doubled down, noting that Republicans have been highlighting his full name—Abdulrahman—just as they used to surround “Barack Hussein Obama” with scare quotes. (Trump, a leading proponent of the conspiracy theory that Obama was born in Africa, still does this.)

Efforts to replicate the former president’s mien can also risk coming off like imitation—or, worse, parody. Shapiro’s cadence, inflection, and conspicuous use of the pregnant pause have long invited comparisons to Obama’s speaking style, not all of them positive. “It’s like if I tried to do a really bad impression of Barack Obama,” Vice President J.D. Vance has said. Shapiro is an electoral juggernaut—polls show him with an overwhelming lead in an otherwise purple state—so this might not matter much. But it has already become a punch line that could resurface if he runs for president. (“Barack Obama is the greatest orator of my lifetime,” Shapiro said when asked about the parallels in 2024, denying that he’d ever intentionally emulated the former president.)

Seeing future standard-bearers through Obama-shaped glasses could also lead the party to some uncomfortable places. Since Trump’s return, candidates perceived as authentic, rough-hewn non-careerists have captured Democrats’ hearts. Obama sure has his charms, but he comes out of a different mold: the Harvard-educated lawyer who pictured himself in the Oval Office from an early age. Republicans seem to be realizing that an Obama redux can be spun into an insult—even as they also seem to be warily looking over their shoulders. When Fox News host Laura Ingraham declared Ossoff the Democrats’ “new Obama” in June, she did not mean it as a compliment. After a rally in which Ossoff made a knowing reference to Natalie Harp, a Trump White House aide with whom the president has a suspiciously close relationship, an administration spokesman blasted the freshman senator as “a cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama.”

There are other downsides to the Obama-replication effort. Voters looking for a president often prize stereotypically masculine traits: Height, a deep voice, a healthy reverence for U.S. military might—all while still seeming chill enough to grab a beer with. Women can have all of those qualities, too, and political science research suggests female candidates often perform as well as or better than male ones. But it’s probably no coincidence that few women have cracked pundits’ list of Obama-like figures. Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whose rapid ascent one Democratic strategist has called “eerily similar” to Obama’s, may be the only exceptions.

Then, of course, there’s the small matter of actually beating Republicans in elections. Voters and consultants looking for an Obama-esque standard-bearer risk over-indexing on certain qualities—an inspiring backstory, an exciting policy agenda, or a smooth jump shot—while underrating others that may resonate beyond die-hard Democrats. As a candidate, Obama had the rare ability to come off like a centrist to centrists and like a progressive to progressives. But he also practiced strategic moderation, publicly opposing same-sex marriage during his first presidential run while both supporting a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who lacked permanent legal status and cracking down on unauthorized border crossings.

In this way, superficial Obama similarities can mask differences that may end up being determinative in the voting booth. El-Sayed has thrilled progressives by supporting Medicare for All and trading insults with Trump—which may also help explain why he’s one of the swing-state Democrats most in danger of losing in November. (Most polls show El-Sayed leading his Republican opponent relatively narrowly even as Democrats in other purple states—including Ossoff, Shapiro, and Roy Cooper in North Carolina—appear comfortably ahead.) El-Sayed has also tolerated controversy to a degree that Obama never did. Confronted during the 2008 campaign with his longtime pastor Jeremiah Wright’s inflammatory comments, Obama cut Wright off, condemned his remarks “in unequivocal terms,” and delivered a speech that transubstantiated the controversy into a public meditation on racism and patriotism. El-Sayed, meanwhile, has repeatedly resisted calls—including from other Democrats—to disavow Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has said that “America deserved 9/11.” (Piker has apologized for that one and El-Sayed called it a “dumb statement,” but Republicans are still trying their darnedest to turn it into a general-election liability.)

There’s also the fact that campaign tactics and political mores have evolved since Obama’s day. The former president has sometimes spiced things up since leaving office, dropping the encomiums to America’s better angels he dispensed when he was on the ballot. At the 2024 Democratic National Convention, Obama suggested that Trump’s “weird obsession with crowd sizes” might have something to do with his anatomy. Still, Ossoff’s recent dig at Harp, which uncorked a geyser of speculation that she and the president may be having an affair, was a notably un-Obama-like move. David Axelrod, the former president’s onetime chief strategist, called it “gratuitous and unnecessary.” But Ossoff’s remark also commanded attention, feeding a boomlet that helped bump up his standing in polls of the hypothetical 2028 presidential primary. If the high horse Obama successfully rode into the White House is truly dead, Democrats who pretend otherwise risk getting outflanked.

Last, all the Obama comparisons in the world won’t help Democrats figure out whether his technocratic, center-left brand of institutionalism remains the governing approach the party should adopt the next time it holds power in Washington. Obama himself has acknowledged that politics has changed since he left. “If I were running today, I wouldn’t run the same race or have the same platform as I did in 2008,” he said in 2020. The next Democratic congressional majority and the next Democratic president will have to make choices about which issues to prioritize and how far to push them: climate or healthcare, incremental progress or sweeping overhaul, policy or institutional change. In a sense, this is just the latest rejoinder in an ongoing fight. The 2020 Democratic primary was riven by debates over whether to build on Obama’s incremental progress on healthcare or start afresh with something like Medicare for All.

That time, the pro-Obama wing won the argument, but Trump’s return has even moderate Democrats wondering if it’s time to try the other path. “It showed me the need for institutional change,” Buttigieg recently told NOTUS of his time working for Biden. “Democrats can’t take us back to the early 2020s or the 2010s,” he added. “We shouldn’t try.” Other Democrats weighing presidential runs are looking even further back in time. “I’m an FDR Democrat,” Rep. Ro Khanna of California said this week in New Hampshire. “I’m a Democrat who believes that this party needs to do big things again.”

Amid all the hagiography, Obama’s record warrants some scrutiny. Some of his achievements, most notably the Affordable Care Act, still stand. But his presidency didn’t come close to solving structural issues that still plague the party today, from a gerrymandered House to a Senate tilted toward Republican-dominated states. And in Obama’s choices and temperament—from not passing a more generous economic stimulus and not pressuring Ruth Bader Ginsburg to step down from the Supreme Court to privately anointing Hillary Clinton as his preferred successor in 2016—there’s a case to be made that the 44th president bears some responsibility for the paroxysms of the Trump years.

So if not the next Obama, who should Democrats be looking for? To answer that, it’s worth going back to seventh grade social studies. Even as my teacher whispered about him excitedly, Obama was far from the consensus choice. Back then, Democrats had a different broadly successful two-term president to look back on. Hillary wasn’t Bill; her 2008 campaign took pains to emphasize their differences. But she was literally another Clinton, and as late as January 2008 commanded nearly double Obama’s support among Democratic primary voters. Yet those same voters ended up rejecting a Clintonian retread—and holding the White House for the next eight years. There’s a clear lesson there.

Ultimately, trying to clone Obama is likely to be a fool’s errand. He’s a pretty singular figure. So rather than fixating on candidates who resemble him in mannerisms or policy, Democrats might instead try to find someone who can do what he did: Give them a new way to think about politics that was so transformative that the party is still pining for it nearly 20 years later. As Obama memorably put it once upon a time, “Change will not come if we wait for some other person or if we wait for some other time. We are the ones we’ve been waiting for.”
news.summary: El-Sayed. Ossoff. Buttigieg? Talarico! The list goes on and on.

news.title: The Amazing Movement Against Data Centers, plus How to Be a Dissident
news.text:
Jon Wiener: From The Nation magazine, this is Start Making Sense. I’m Jon Wiener. Later in the hour: How to be a dissident in an age of fear – Ami Fields-Meyer has thought a lot about that. He’s co-author of the new book “On Courage.” But first: a new kind of mass politics in America—David Wallace-Wells will explain–in a minute.[BREAK]Jon Wiener: Is the resistance to data centers a new kind of mass politics in America? David Wallace-Wells has been thinking about that. He’s a writer for The New York Times Opinion Pages, a columnist for The New York Times Magazine, and author of the unforgettable book The Uninhabitable Earth. David Wallace-Wells, welcome to the program.

David Wallace-Wells: Great to be here. Thanks for having me.

JW: I have to confess that I ignored the protests against data centers when they emerged a few months ago. I thought of them just as the latest outburst of Nimby politics — Not in my backyard — seeking to preserve an America that doesn’t exist for a lot of people. And I thought the challenges would be easily resolved by building data centers in places that welcomed economic growth. Maybe I thought a few candidates looking for an issue would demand concessions from the companies, and maybe they’d get some minor ones. But Microsoft and Amazon Web Services are just too powerful for a handful of towns to resist. So, I was feeling pretty uninterested in those protests. You’ve written that you felt sort of the same way, you once called the movement against data centers “a pretty quixotic way of fighting the progress of AI.” How are you feeling about that way of fighting right now?

DWW: Well, I feel shamed by what has transpired, against my own expectations. Precisely because I was so fatalistic, as I take it you were, about how limited the ability of citizens to take control of this story really was. Six or 9 months ago, I was already seeing polling suggesting that the American public was really uncomfortable, wary, frustrated, even angry about the mass infrastructure build-out to serve AI. You saw some quite dramatic jumps over the course of the fall into the winter in public opinion polls. And you saw a lot of small scale, but quite impressive protest activity at the level of town halls and that sort of thing. But I, myself, I looked at that problem and ran the math the same way that you did and thought, ‘we do not live in a healthy political economy in which citizens can exert control over the powers that shape our lives very reliably.’ Most people know that that is one source of political frustration, that they have already learned that lesson over many hard years. And so even if AI now looms as a new challenge, which they see as larger or more urgent than previous things that motivated them to get out and protest, the end result was likely to be pretty similar, which is to say, an expression of outrage and disgust, followed by victory on behalf of the corporations who have the most skin in the game. And I have to say, I don’t know for sure that that story won’t play out in precisely those terms going forward. 

I think you know that it is, and by any measure, the data center build-out is not just continuing but accelerating. In many cases, when there has been pushback and projects have been canceled, as you suggest, they move to friendlier locations. And I think over the longer term, even if this really grows into a genuine national movement in which it becomes almost impossible to build anywhere, I do think that much of that work can be done abroad, which means if you understand the objection primarily as anxiety about artificial intelligence and its march of progress through all of our lives, then I don’t know how much this movement is really going to change that trajectory ultimately.But just at the level of political organization, coalition building and consensus building, I think what we have seen is the most astonishing development in American politics since the rise of MAGA. Maybe you could draw it further back to Occupy and the Tea Party before that. And in a certain way, casting your eyes back further into history. Because the truth is, we’re now at a point when 75% of the country objects to the construction of data centers, and that is in their own backyards. And that is a level of consensus that we just haven’t seen on almost any issue for a very long time.

JW: I just want to pause on that figure. Tell us that again.

DWW: 75% of Americans say that they do not want data centers built in their own communities. And, on one on the one hand, you can look at that and think of it as NIMBYism, and NIMBYism is a part of it. People don’t want these things built in their backyards. They don’t want the local pollution effects. They don’t want the eyesore of construction. They don’t want their small towns being shadowed by a giant data center whose inner workings they don’t understand, run for the profit and benefit of corporations which don’t understand them. All of those things are factors in this, in this resistance.But it’s also the case that 55% of Americans believe in a national data center moratorium. They believe that no data center should be built anywhere in the country, 55%, which means at least that share of the coalition is not objecting on a NIMBY basis, because they’re not saying, ‘I don’t want this in my backyard.’ They’re saying, ‘I don’t want this anywhere in this country, even if it’s hundreds of miles from the closest town. We don’t want to do this at all.’More than half of the country now believes that, and it’s especially striking, that 75% figure, when you compare it to other things that people have raised NIMBY objections to. I’m a climate person. I’ve written a lot and thought a lot about the struggles to build renewable energy. And over the last few months, you’ve heard a lot of people raising comparisons between the anti-data center movement and the anti-renewable movement. And there is some overlap there. They share some people. They share some rhetoric. But more than two-thirds of Americans want solar farms built in their backyards. And more than two-thirds of Americans don’t want data centers built in their backyards.So, we’re seeing something that is really divergent, different in category and scale from any comparable movement of the last decade or two. And that, I think is really notable, significant, and should make people like you and me really reflect on what we’re seeing here, what it tells us about where we are, and especially what it tells us about where we’re heading.

JW: What do we know about who is in this 75%? Who are these people?

DWW: Everybody. That’s the short answer. I mean, you can divide this country by – certainly by partisanship Republicans are a little bit friendlier to data centers than Democrats, but there are something like 40 or 50 points underwater with Republicans. So, they may be 80 points underwater with Democrats, but we’re still talking about a huge, huge opposition all across the political aisle, centrist to independents.You can divide the country by education level, by income, whether you live in an urban area or a rural area, whether you got a college degree or you’re just a high school graduate or didn’t finish high school. Every single subcategory that you can divide the country by will show a significant opposition to data center construction, at least in one’s own local community. And that is I mean, just put aside the issue itself, put aside what it tells us about policy. It is just an astonishing fact. In 2026, given how divided we are about absolutely everything, that this is something that the entire country has rallied around despite the fact that our politicians are, well, they’re now belatedly kind of climbing on board to the movement. But up until a few months ago, you almost couldn’t find a national leader who was speaking really forthrightly, really directly, really dramatically against data centers. So, on some level, this is a truly grassroots movement as well. And I think just as astonishing or even more astonishing on that basis.

JW: Tell us a little bit about not just the extent of support in opinion polls, but the concrete goals that have already been achieved by this movement in just the last couple of months. You have these figures about the number of jurisdictions that have passed bans, the situation in state politics. What do we know about all that?

DWW: Yeah, I mean, in general, what we’re seeing is something that is much more developed at the local level. And you’ve seen hundreds of data center moratoriums passed by local jurisdictions over the last few months.

JW: You say 500.

DWW: Yeah. And in certain states where I remember reading and reporting about Maryland something like 80% of Maryland is now covered by data center moratorium. So even when you hear local level restrictions, they can really add up and become a quite significant barrier to construction. We now have in New York the first state level moratorium, which was signed by Kathy Hochul maybe two months ago. And in the relatively recent past, you’ve had something – they’re not – they’re technically not moratoriums in the same way, but something like that being implemented by executive order, by both the governors of Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro, and the governor of Texas, Greg Abbott. And both of those seem really quite significant to me, culturally, because we think of Kathy Hochul as an ally of Zohran, who’s navigating the centrist left wing divide in the Democratic Party relatively nimbly. She’s got her finger in the wind. She’s following some trends.Josh Shapiro is someone who has made his name as a national politician, as a kind of “I’m going to get stuff done.” That’s his catchphrase. He’s proud of plowing through environmental review and suspending all of these restrictions on construction projects. That’s how he got the I-95 bridge fixed so quickly. And he presents himself as a kind of abundance, technocratic centrist, “get it done” liberal. And as recently as six months ago, was personally celebrating large-scale data center projects in the state of Pennsylvania. On that basis, according to that logic. And now he’s come out and said, “I’m not going to be bullied and intimidated by these big corporations who don’t have the interest of Pennsylvanians at heart. We need to pause this. We need to slow this down. We need to make sure, absolutely sure that these projects are serving the communities in which they’re built. And in the meantime, we’re going to not do any more of them politically.”

JW: I thought of this as more a Democratic issue than a Republican one, and it’s not that surprising that Josh Shapiro would join in. But you say Greg Abbott is also part of this. What do we know about Republican opposition to data centers?

DWW: I mean, to trust the survey data, it is overwhelming. To trust the on-the-ground reporting at protests, which is to say, not just people who tell a pollster that they don’t want a data center in their backyard, but people who are willing to go out and scream at their local town council about it. Some significant share of the objections are familiar from our understanding of the MAGA and MAHA right. In fact, there’s a relatively serious stream of influence from the MAGA right into the data center resistance. Steve Bannon has been an especially pronounced prominent critic of AI and data center build-out. And he has a number of prominent followers who are regular guests on his show, who are now relatively central parts of the coalition. And if you’re interested in that, you can read, there’s a great piece by Molly Taft in Wired, a few weeks ago, documenting that right-wing part of the coalition. I wouldn’t say that it’s dominant. It still seems to me most of the people who are objecting to the extent that they identify politically are left of center, and they do front load their environmental concerns. They often talk about worries about climate and emissions. And so, for all those reasons, I do think there’s probably a heavier liberal anchor to the coalition.

JW: But Texas — Texas is a place that has portrayed itself as the ultimate utopia of unchecked corporate power. And yet you say Greg Abbott has issued what amounts to a moratorium.

DWW: Yeah. I mean, I would go even further than in your setup than to say it’s unchecked corporate power. I mean, I hear a lot from people in the climate world that Texas is an enviable place to build clean energy because they’re so hands off. And that’s the reason why Texas is now building so much more renewable capacity than California. It’s not because Texans care more about climate change. It’s not even because they care more about their electricity bills. It’s just because the regulatory environment is so much more permissive. You can build whatever you want in Texas. And so, when they’re renewable developers who see all the capacity, all the possibility for solar and wind, they can just stand up that new infrastructure quite quickly. Whereas in many other states, particularly blue states, it’s a little bit harder.So, it’s not just about handing over the keys to the corporations, it’s about letting anybody do whatever they want. Now, in this case, a lot of corporations want to build data centers for the exact same reasons that they want to build solar farms and wind power, which is to say it can get done more quickly. There’s less oversight. And there’s also a lot of booming demand in Texas for – that’s where some of the companies are based. And in fact, some of the biggest projects in America have been based in Texas as a result. But there has been a really significant backlash on the ground there. So much so that, yes, this incredibly outspoken right-wing governor is not just putting a pause on data center development. He’s talking about that pause in terms that would be familiar at any town hall in the country. He’s saying we need to prioritize Texans first. There’s a big rallying cry among the anti-AI movement “humans first.” And Greg Abbott is saying “we need to put Texans first,” he said, “we need to ensure that all of these projects meet our own environmental standards, so we’re not polluting the local environment.” This is a state where it’s like any – you can build a petrochemical plant in Cancer Alley. Nobody cares. But he’s willing to make a stand against environmental toxins in the context of data centers, too. And I think that is because the data that he’s looking at, the survey information that he’s seeing, shows him that this is not a vocal fringe who are really raising their voices loudly. It is a set of worries, interlinked, sometimes contradictory, but a patchwork set of worries that are shared to some degree by the large majority of even his loyal constituents. And when a politician, a professional politician, sees that dynamic, they simply can’t ignore it, even if they’re kind of godfather, Trump in DC, is more interested in serving the needs of Silicon Valley oligarchs who are committed to him. Those who are closer to the ground, more responsive to local constituents, have to recognize that there is an enormous backlash brewing of a scale and a kind that we, as I said, really haven’t seen in America for quite a long time.

JW: We also have to talk about Ohio here. Ground zero for the politics of data centers right now is the Ohio Senate race where Sherrod Brown is running against Jon Husted. A couple of weeks ago, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that Democrats have made data centers the centerpiece of their Senate campaign in Ohio and that it is working. The latest Fox News poll has Sherrod Brown eight points ahead, and his ads call his opponent “the face of data centers,” which is true in Ohio. Do you think the Republicans will be able to recover from this in Ohio?

DWW: Well, I think each of these races, as all political races, are multi-determined. It’s not narrowly a – none of these races are going to be determined exclusively by data center resistance, but I do think that it’s a benefit to be at least in support of a moratorium, if not an outright ban, and those who are more committed to building out the infrastructure in a more aggressive way and are on record doing so are going to be political losers as a result.And that is a problem not just for Republicans in Ohio. It’s a problem for basically every incumbent politician anywhere in the country, because up until quite recently, this seemed like the sort of deal that most politicians would intuitively take, which is to say, you may have to waive some tax breaks in front of a developer to get them to locate their project in your neck of the woods. But it was also a meaningful economic boom which they assumed that voters would appreciate, particularly if, as you said at the top, some of the sort of particular concerns were addressed.Now, that no longer seems to be the logic, but it was so intuitively the logic to leaders that – Kamala Harris was running promising tax breaks for data centers in 2020 for not producing a significant backlash in the public because it was one of those kind of bipartisan consensus issues that this is a way to reindustrialize the country.

DWW: It’s a way to revive union labor work that we lament losing in other areas, as well as sort of securing more of a national foothold in the technological future. Again, this is the kind of like if we’re checking boxes, this is something that checks the box for every centrist politician out there. And as a result, they were all, broadly speaking, supportive. Even if they had some, they were picking up on some AI anxiety from their constituents. Now we’re in the absolute opposite position. The consensus bipartisan perspective is not to support this build out. It’s to oppose it. And that is especially striking, given that – to the extent that we can measure whether those that political that economic political calculation I just mentioned cashed out. That is to say, to the extent that we can measure whether the data center projects that have been built to this point were economic booms to their local communities. There are many really positive, powerful cases where there were huge benefits. I mean, in Loudoun County, which is an incredibly rich place, it’s the richest county in the United States.

JW: Loudoun County, Virginia, just south of Washington, D.C.

DWW: People often say “if the rich people really like data centers, they should build them in their own backyards.” Actually, they are building them — in the richest county in the country, more than anywhere else in the country. And in Loudoun County, they’re expecting more than half of their tax revenues to come directly from data centers as recently as the next few years.

JW: And this could be a big thing in poor counties, too.

DWW: Oh, absolutely. And there are examples of that. I mean, in the piece I mentioned in Richland Parish, Louisiana, they gave $50,000 bonuses to elementary school teachers, none of whom make $50,000 in salary, because of the construction of the metadata center. And there are, I wouldn’t say countless many projects are not negotiated, were not negotiated in this way. And so don’t have such concrete benefits to offer. But if you were like in a position at a town hall trying to make the case to your local constituents, there are a number of examples to point to or say, ‘we can get a deal from these developers where like, we’re going to get a new high school, we’re going to get a new emergency response system. We’re going to have a huge boost in our property tax revenues, so much so that we can count on cutting your taxes over the next decade or so. We can promise all of those promises. We can extract those promises in writing.’ And even with that pitch, nobody in the country is interested. And that, to me, is among the most astonishing and impressive things about this movement.On some level, I’m even ambivalent about it, because I do think that the benefits to local communities and poor areas can be quite significant, but as a pure expression of political refusal.As I keep saying, we just have not seen anything like this in America ever before. That kind of a deal that they’re offering should be the sweet spot in American politics. It’s what we were told was the sweet spot in American politics. ‘We’re going to improve your public services, and you get to pay less in taxes.’ But the people who are hearing that pitch don’t trust the people making it. They, and to the extent that they trust that there will be some benefits, they simply don’t believe that they should outweigh all of the costs that they’re tabulating in their minds, from water stress to electricity prices to the strain on the community, the degradation of the natural environment all the way down to “we’re worried about what AI is going to do to our children’s brains, and, the way that it will supercharge the surveillance state.” And they tally up all those things and they tally up the concrete benefits in terms of tax revenue and improved social services. And they say, “I’m not going to take that deal.” I’m kind of in awe of that.

JW: Let’s just spend a minute on Trump’s remark that the people who oppose data centers want to be “backwards and poor.”

DWW: When I hear Donald Trump saying those things, I feel a little tickle of glee that he is completely — he’s been boxed in and outflanked, and misunderstands the country for whom he has presented himself as a kind of a tribune now for a decade. When I look at the data, I see some of the same math that Trump does, and I see local communities refusing payouts that would change the landscape of their lives, but they’re also refusing to have a future dominated by artificial intelligence imposed on them from above, without their input. And he thinks, wait, I don’t really know that much about NATO. So, he Googles NATO and he realizes it’s this all for one and one for all pact. And he goes to ChatGPT. I think that shame is a limited political tool, and I think that we can use it in the context of public leaders, but for the most part, shaming people into submission, normal people, day to day people who are just trying to live their lives doesn’t work. What are the other ways to do this? One of the ways is to help people arrive at what we call in the book, a moral collision. To help people get to their own breaking point, where they feel what you have once, what you once felt, which was, I can no longer stay silent on this or anything else.One of my favorite stories from history on this comes from Mississippi Freedom Summer. And what we know from that moment was that there was a big fight, a big argument between Fannie Lou Hamer, the Black woman activist on the ground in Mississippi, and the national leadership of SNCC Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. And what we know from this story is that there was a big argument in around 1964 about while they were trying to push for the Voting Rights Act, whether to bring in, whether to include white northern students, some of whom were sort of on the fence and some of whom were interested but didn’t yet have really a clear entry point into the movement. And the SNCC people on up in Washington, D.C., said, “that’s going to dilute our movement.” And the folks on the ground said, “are you kidding? Every time we bring down white students, we get more press, more media. DOJ has a bigger presence here. It’s a little bit sAFMer for us. And more people will get to understand what’s going on.” So, she won. They won out. And as a result, you saw busloads of white students show up in Mississippi that summer as part of the ultimately successful push for the Voting Rights Act.And what they witnessed – they witnessed so much brutality against their Black peers for simply trying to exercise their constitutional rights, that many of them were radicalized and became members of this movement in ways that were helpful. Unfortunately, it was necessary at that point to win people over.But the other most interesting part of this, and I think even more relevant to your question, is that the other knock-on effect that we hear less about was that many of their parents were also moved. These were people who were much more obstinate, much more stubborn, much less likely to join or become sympathetic to the civil rights movement. We need to get people involved. We need to bring people to the brink of their own moral collisions. And we need to make sure that the arms of a movement are waiting to catch them when they’re ready, whenever it is that they’re ready. As difficult a proposition as this is for my friends and peers, it’s really, really, really important work. And we see that from all over the world.

JW: One last thing: let’s talk about fun and humor and joy in dissident movements.

AFM: You know, I think that joy is a beachhead for organizing. Being part of a movement gives you a lot of agency. It’s not always so serious. It’s not always so dire. Everything is ultimately about fighting for justice. But what we see in many, many places is that making it fun for people and making it enjoyable for people gives people a way.And I’ll tell one other story on this, which is also actually from Syria, but it is during the Milosevic era, sorry, from Serbia, but it is during the Milosevic era, which is that they were, as protesters at that time were protesting and pushing back against Milosevic’s corruption. They brought a barrel with Milosevic’s face into a town square to a city square. And they said you could pay two dinars, to hit his face on the barrel. And if you didn’t have enough money, you could hit him twice. And so, the point was all about how Milosevic was stealing all your money. And eventually the police showed up and confiscated the barrel, because you’re not supposed to make fun of the authoritarian. And the movement in response, put out a press release that said this: “See, this is how repressive Milosevic is. He even arrested a barrel.”There is tremendous power in giving people joy. We need many, many ways in. Some of those will be moral collisions. Some of those will be giving people a role in your movement. But sometimes that’s just going to be inviting people to something where they’re going to have fun and feel connected and feel a little bit more agency in the work.

JW: Ami Fields-Meyer. His new book is On Courage: How to Be a Dissident in an Age of Fear. Rachel Maddow called it “a classic for our time” and decided she wanted to read the audio book. Ami, thanks for all your work – and thanks for talking with us today.

AFM: Thank you, Jon, it’s such a pleasure.

news.title: Jimmy Kimmel launches vicious tirade against Trump in first episode back from summer break... while ignoring reports show is set to end next year
news.text:
Jimmy Kimmel unleashed on President Trump in his first show back from summer break - just hours after reports his late-night run is coming to an end next year. 

The comedian returned to the stage Tuesday night for the first time in three months, marking his return from summer hiatus and the 4,000th episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live. 

Sources told Page Six that his 24-year television run is set to end in 2027, but insisted his criticism of Trump was unlikely to be the reason. 

Kimmel, 58, remained silent on the reports, instead turning his 15-minute monologue into a blistering attack on the president.

'Donald Trump and I have one thing in common,' he told the audience. 'We both accomplished nothing all summer long.'

The late-night host spent the segment running through moments involving Trump and the White House, claiming that when he left for vacation in June, the 'country was a mess.' 

He rattled off the war with Iran, soaring gas prices, high inflation and Kentucky Senator Mitch McConnell, who 'was either alive or dead, nobody seemed to have any idea which.' 

Kimmel then mocked Trump's botched $20 million Reflecting Pool makeover, branding the landmark a 'big green slop hole' while showing images of its murky green waters. 

'Now, only three months later, I'm so pleased to report that thanks to your favorite president, DJ Jazzy Donald, every one of those problems has been solved, we made America great again!' the comedian said sarcastically.

Earlier this week, the Reflecting Pool found itself in yet another mess after powerful storms left the landmark surrounded by toppled fencing, fallen trees, dirty rainwater and debris - just days after Trump claimed it was 'almost completely fixed.'

It was the latest setback for a project that began in April to repair the pool and turn it 'American Flag Blue' - a renovation the White House said would take just a few weeks. 

'The president had three months, spent 20 million dollars and couldn't even get a pool cleaned,' Kimmel said during Tuesday's show, before showing recent photos of the Reflecting Pool covered in tarps and seemingly filled with dark liquid.

'I thought he was supposed to drain the swamp, he turned it into gravy instead,' he said, joking that perhaps Trump was pumping the pool with Diet Coke instead - a quip that drew laughter from the crowd.

'How are we supposed to win the war with Iran when we can't even win the war against algae for God sake,' the comedian added.

Kimmel then turned his focus to Trump's popularity with Americans, declaring: 'Trump's poll numbers and pool numbers are at all-time lows. Only 33 percent.'

He claimed that with just one in three registered voters approving of his job performance, the president is doing everything he can to 'keep us from voting in the midterms.'

Kimmel then stunned the crowd with a joke about 35-year-old Natalie Harp, one of Trump's top personal aides, after her intimate handwritten letters to the president were revealed - including one that read: 'You are all that matters to me.'

'Would a president with historically low popularity number play golf instead of working over the weekend?' Kimmel said. 

'I don't know, would Natalie Harp drive a golf cart in high heels? You bet your chicken tenders they would,' he added, as an image of Harp driving a golf cart in heels flashed behind him.

The host then zeroed in on the week's biggest developments: 'On Friday, fuel prices hit an all-time high. The Strait of Hormuz is still closed... at this point, Blockbuster Video has a better chance of reopening than the Strait of Hormuz,' he said.

Kimmel said Trump, who declared victory on the first day of the war nearly six-and-a-half months ago, is now dismissing the ongoing conflict as 'small potatoes.' 

'No one knows more about small potatoes than a man who is built like a sack of wet tater tots,' he joked.

With Tuesday's episode airing just after Labor Day weekend, Kimmel flashed a 2024 post from Trump in which he claimed Americans were suffering through the holiday thanks to Kamala Harris.

At the time, the president wrote: 'Under Comrade Kamala Harris, all Americans are suffering during this Holiday weekend - High Gas Prices, Transportation Costs are up and Grocery Prices are through the roof.'

'We can't keep living under this weak and failed "Leadership..."' Trump added.

In response, Kimmel pointed to gas prices on Labor Day 2024 under Harris, which he said stood at $3.33 a gallon. Now, he said, prices have ballooned to $4.15 a gallon - the highest Labor Day gas prices in US history. 

He described Trump as 'crazier than ever,' pointing to the barrage of AI-generated images flooding his social media feeds and noting that he posted 37 times on Sunday alone. 

Kimmel's heated monologue ended with a compilation video of what he called the best and worst moments of Trump's summer 2026, before the main show finally got underway.

Tuesday's show followed the shocking news that the decades-long late-night run is reportedly set to end in 2027, according to Page Six.

An insider told the publication: 'His contract is not getting extended.' Kimmel was famously suspended by the network a year earlier.

In a statement to the Daily Mail, a spokesperson for ABC Entertainment said: 'This information is inaccurate - any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative.' 

One insider claimed that new Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro wouldn't be influenced by pressure from Trump and his supporters.

'He’s not afraid of the administration… Josh isn’t folding,' they claimed.

Another source at ABC claimed that a desire to cut costs may have influenced the network to not renew Kimmel's contract, stating: 'It wouldn’t have anything to do with Trump.'

D'Amaro was also reportedly offering early-retirement packages to executives as part of a restructuring and push to cut costs.

news.title: SAVE America Act vs. Packing Supreme Court: Devil in the Details
news.text:
STAR PARKER

FOR RELEASE: WEDNESDAY, SEPT. 9, 2026

SAVE America Act v. Packing Supreme Court: Devil in the Details

In February 2026, the U.S. House passed the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility America Act to require proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and an approved form of government photo ID to cast a ballot.

Every House Republican voted for the SAVE America Act, but every Democrat except one voted against this election integrity measure.

When the Senate sought to consider the House-passed bill in March 2026, every Republican supported the proposal, and every Democrat opposed it. The unanimous opposition of Democrats prevented the Senate from attaining the 60 votes needed under Senate rules and the bill failed to proceed.

President Donald Trump and many conservative activists have urged Senate Republicans to invoke a procedural "nuclear option" to change the Senate rules so that the SAVE America Act and all legislation can proceed with a simple majority.

Many Senate Republicans, including several of its most conservative members, oppose lowering the 60-vote threshold. They believe it will damage the institution's deliberative nature and make it harder to block extreme Democratic legislation when there is a Democratic president with House and Senate majorities.

While many conservatives have vented their frustration against Senate Republicans, Democrats see another villain thwarting their efforts to implement an increasingly liberal agenda: the Republican-appointed majority on the U.S. Supreme Court.

On Sept. 2, 2026, the House voted on a proposed constitutional amendment to keep nine justices on the U.S. Supreme Court — the number for the past 157 years. The "Keep 9" proposal comes as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is saying "everything is on the table" to deal with a Supreme Court majority that Democrats find objectionable.

Former House Majority Whip James Clyburn, D-S.C, called for adding four justices to the Supreme Court in a recent "Meet the Press" interview. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., have called for adding at least four new seats to the Court. California Gov. Gavin Newson is "warming to the idea."

The views on court-packing expressed by these current Democrat leaders stand in stark contrast to those of Clinton-appointed Former Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who opposed court-packing.

In 1983, then-Sen. Joe Biden called President Franklin D. Roosevelt's 1937 attempt at court-packing a "bonehead idea" and a "terrible, terrible mistake." During a presidential primary debate in 2019, Biden said adding more justices to the Supreme Court would destroy "any credibility the Court has at all."

Conservative opponents of the Democrats' court-packing scheme argue that Democrats and their liberal activists want a Supreme Court that will view the Constitution as a "living, breathing document" that can be interpreted to impose a far-left agenda on America.

The next time there is a Democratic president and Democratic majorities in Congress, many conservatives believe they will eliminate the Senate's 60-vote requirement to enact a wish list of liberal legislation. This list will include a national election law that overrides every photo ID, citizenship verification or clean voter rolls requirement that Republicans have been able to pass at the state or federal level.

The House vote on the "Keep 9" amendment fell short of the two-thirds needed to advance a constitutional amendment. Consistent with their votes against the SAVE America Act, only one Democrat voted to "Keep 9" while 205 voted against it.

The independence of the Supreme Court must be preserved from a future Congress and president manipulating its size for political gain. And size does matter: the smaller the size, the less opportunity for stalemates or legislating from the bench.

Republicans and their conservative allies should recognize who their real opponents are and turn their attention to an election that is less than two months away.

And voters should know these details behind the debate to discern differences between the SAVE America Act and packing the Supreme Court before they decide which party should control our Congress come November.

Star Parker is founder of the Center for Urban Renewal and Education and author of "Necessary Noise, How Donald Trump Inflames the Culture War and Why this is Good News for America" (Hachette 2019).
