news.title: Dems, GOP go with safer bets in NH Senate primaries: 3 takeaways
news.text:
New Hampshire voters on both sides of the aisle made the safer bet Sept. 8 in what could be a quietly consequential battle for the U.S. Senate this fall.

Within minutes of the polls closing, results were called for the Democratic and Republican nominations for Senate, which easily went to Rep. Chris Pappas and former Sen. John E. Sununu, respectively.

The GOP is hoping to fortify their 53-47 Senate majority against a forecasted "blue wave" in the 2026 midterms and many believe one of their best options is in the Granite State, where retiring Democratic incumbent Jeanne Shaheen has left a purple state wide open.

Recruiting Sununu was a big get for the GOP, which is promising to spend $17 million in the state this year to flip the seat. He comes from a popular family in the state and served in the Senate previously, having defeated Jeanne Shaheen in 2002 before losing their rematch six years later.

"We need to shake up Washington with real reform," Sununun said during his victory speech Tuesday.

Pappas alluded to Democratic anxiety about the race during his speech, saying it will be a tough contest over the next eight weeks that will require "everyone under the tent" to win this fall.

Kyle Kondik, managing editor of the nonpartisan Sabato's Crystal Ball newsletter at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, said Democrats are still favored to hold the seat November.

"This is ultimately a Democratic-leaning state in federal races, and this is a Democratic leaning year," he said. "That is a lot for Sununu to overcome."

Further down the ballot was a race to fill Pappas' seat, which on the Democratic side featured a familiar name with Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of the outgoing senator, taking on Maura Sullivan, a retired Marine, for the nomination in one of the country's swingiest districts.

N.H.'s quiet Senate contest could be deciding factor

Weeks before the primary election Pappas and Sununu were already acting as if the general election was the only contest by largely ignoring their intra-party rivals.

That's in part because both sides understand the importance of New Hampshire, which former Vice President Kamala Harris won by a little less than three percentage points in 2024.

The GOP is defending six Senate seats this year, including places President Donald Trump won decisively, such as Texas and Iowa. Flipping the Granite State would ease the current heartburn consuming Republicans heading into the fall.

Sununu had the tougher task in defeating Scott Brown, a former Republican senator from Massachusetts who gained national fame in 2010 for winning the seat once held by Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy, a liberal lion.

With Trump's endorsement, Sununu breezed through despite publicly disagreeing with the administration's foreign trade wars and calling the president a "loser" in a 2024 op-ed. He mentioned term limits and members of Congress paying for their own health insurance during his victory speech Tuesday before calling out Pappas' vote last year against ending the government shutdown.

"No more career politicians," Sununu said.

Pappas, who would be the first openly gay male senator if elected, won his primary by holding off a late surge from a more progressive foe. Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist and first-time candidate, supported Medicare for All and abolishing ICE while declining money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

The congressman also outpaced Sununu and Brown combined in terms of fundraising, federal campaign records shows, while being considered the more electable candidate in November by most experts and strategists. He served four terms in the House representing New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District, one of the swingiest in the nation.

Pappas evoked Trump in an attack ad released Tuesday and during his victory speech, calling out how the president's seen his personal wealth balloon by billions since returning to power.

"In fact, he says we're living in a 'golden age'. Well I think he's living on another planet, because does this feel like a golden age to you," Pappas said.

Forecasters rate New Hampshire as leaning Democratic, but polls of a general election matchup between the two show a virtual tie, which means both parties are expected to invest heavily into the state.

Shaheen, Sullivan's razor-thin finish for swing district

Pappas running for Senate left his House seat vacant and that attracted a crowded seven-person field with Maura Sullivan, a retired Marine, and Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of the outgoing senator, at the top.

Sullivan, an Iraq War veteran, and Shaheen, a former city councilor in Portsmouth, both agreed on abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs and pushing to impeach Trump should Democrats take back the House.

But the two jousted over other differences, such as Medicare for All. During one of their debates, for instance, Stefany Shaheen called out Sullivan, who served in the Obama administration, for supporting a plan that would keep private insurance as an option.

As of Tuesday evening, Stefany Shaheen was leading Sullivan by about two percentage points with 71% of precincts reporting.

On the GOP side, businessman Anthony DiLorenzo, a first-time candidate who Trump endorsed, easily prevailed over Hollie Noveletsky.

Covering the southeastern part of the state, New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District has been a presidential election bellwether since 2000.

Midterms featuring nepo-candidates show mixed results

Part of Sullivan's attack strategy was going after Stefany Shaheen's lineage as too privileged.

One 30-second TV spot featured a New Hampshire voter saying he wanted a "fighter, not a fancy last name."

Stefany Shaheen walked a tightrope throughout the campaign, saying at the outset she was "very proud of my mom's service," then later criticizing her mother's role as one eight Senate Democrats who approved a deal ending the 2025 government shutdown.

Other candidates with well-known family names have run in this year's primaries with mixed results, including Sununu's win at the top of the ticket. He is the son and brother of former New Hampshire governors.

Most recently Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., won a special runoff in August after taking the seat held by her brother, Lindsey Graham, who died in July. But other contenders connected to U.S. political dynasties, such as Jack Schlossberg, a grandson of former President John F. Kennedy, have lost their bids.

news.title: Minnesota Senate Race Deadlocked with Democrat and Republican, Poll Shows
news.text: A new poll shows Democrat Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya locked in a close race for Minnesota’s open U.S. Senate seat, with Flanagan holding a narrow 44 percent to 42 percent advantage among likely voters. The two-point gap puts the candidates within a statistical tie, underscoring how competitive the contest could become as the November midterms approach. The poll, conducted by TIPP/League of American Workers from August 31 to September 2 among 1,201 likely voters, also found 4 percent supporting other candidates, while 2 percent said someone else and 8 percent were not sure. The survey comes shortly after both candidates secured their party nominations last month, setting up a general election contest for the seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Tina Smith. The poll has a margin of error of 3 percent. The League of American Workers is not formally affiliated with the Republican Party, but it is a conservative advocacy organization led by former Trump adviser Steve Cortes. Meanwhile, midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the House and Senate, and The Cook Political Report currently rates the race as likely Democrat. Former Vice President Kamala Harris also won the state by roughly 4 points in the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump. Flanagan campaign spokesperson Lexi Byler told Newsweek via email on Tuesday when reached for comment about the new poll, "Michele Tafoya would be nothing but a loyal soldier to Donald Trump. She supports his ICE and mass deportation agenda that led to two Minnesotans being killed, defended January 6 rioters who assaulted police officers and tried to overturn a free and fair election, and supports Trump’s reckless tariffs that are hammering farmers and driving up prices for everyone. Tafoya even told Minnesotans to just 'keep a stiff upper lip' with the higher prices due to Trump’s illegal war in Iran and praised the One Big Beautiful Bill that is ripping health care away from hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans." "Michele Tafoya is fighting for what Trump wants, Peggy Flanagan is fighting for what working families need – Minnesotans know that and it’s why they will choose Peggy Flanagan in November," the statement concluded. Newsweek reached out to Tafoya's campaign via email on Tuesday for comment, and while she did not respond before publication time, she responded to the poll on X, saying, "Our race is in play! Minnesotans are fed up with billions in taxpayer dollars being stolen while the people in charge refuse to take responsibility. Peggy Flanagan is the sitting lieutenant governor while criminals were stealing billions from Minnesota taxpayers. She doesn’t get to walk away from that record. Minnesotans deserve accountability. They deserve leadership. And they deserve better. This race is wide open. Let’s win it!" What To Know Flanagan, Minnesota's lieutenant governor, entered the general election as the Democratic nominee after defeating Representative Angie Craig in the party's primary. Flanagan’s defeat of Craig marked a victory for the Democratic Party’s more progressive wing, which has seen several candidates prevail in recent primaries. Flanagan was considered the more progressive candidate in the contest and received backing from Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, making the race another example of the ongoing divide between progressive and moderate Democrats. Tafoya, a former longtime NFL sideline reporter, won the Republican nomination and is seeking to turn her name recognition and political outsider profile into a statewide victory. The race has drawn national attention as Republicans look to make gains in Minnesota, even though Democrats have maintained a strong statewide advantage in recent elections. The latest numbers are particularly notable because earlier polling also showed Flanagan ahead, although by a somewhat larger margin. The new survey suggests Tafoya may have narrowed the gap as the general election campaign gets underway. Still, a two-point advantage is not enough to establish a clear favorite, particularly with two months remaining before Election Day. According to the poll, Flanagan has more of the Gen-Z, Millennial, female, Black and Hispanic vote. Tafoya has more support from those age 45-years-old and up, men, and white likely voters. Both have 37 percent of the independent vote. Among registered voters Flanagan also has a 2-point lead over Tafoya with 40 percent to 38 percent. That questioned polled 1,494 registered voters and has a margin of error of 2.7 percent. Tafoya has a 34 percent favorable rating compared to a 30 percent unfavorable rating, the poll shows, while 36 percent have no opinion. Flanagan's favorability rating is 39 percent compared to a 34 percent unfavorable rating and 28 percent have no opinion. The survey also asked respondents about Flanagan's position on gender transitions for minors and their potential support. No similar or direct policy question was asked about Tafoya. For now, the latest poll points to a race that could be competitive, with Flanagan and Tafoya separated by just two percentage points and both campaigns facing an opportunity to persuade the relatively small share of voters who have yet to settle on a candidate. Polymarket shows a similar finding on Monday afternoon, with Flanagan having a 94 percent chance to Tafoya's 8 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas

news.title: GOP to rail against ‘socialist’ Dems at Dallas midterm convention — as some fear ‘Trump-a-Palooza’ backlash
news.text:
DALLAS — Republicans are flocking to Texas for an unprecedented national midterm convention headlined by President Trump to turn out voters in the congressional races that will dictate the course of his final two years in office — though some Republicans are nervous it could backfire.

The two-day gathering — nicknamed “Trump-a-Palooza” — offers free publicity for Republicans as they attempt to brand Democrats as “socialists” and features a slew of fundraising events to help the party boost its already large cash advantage to beat back bleak polls pointing to a possible November wipeout.

Trump will speak on Wednesday and Thursday night after 9 p.m. eastern time — with Vice President JD Vance also giving remarks Thursday. 

Earlier slots will feature Trump administration officials touting policy wins and give lesser-known figures a moment in the spotlight to court donors and build momentum before a national audience.

Many speakers plan to frame the election as a choice between Trump’s record and the ascendant socialist wing of the Democratic Party, sources said, as Republicans try to defy the historical trend of a president’s party losing seats in a midterm.

“It’s electrifying. People are excited. People are ready to go,” Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters told conservative media personality Benny Johnson Tuesday, predicting that as many as 60,000 people will show up, including approved members of the public.

“We have 109 speakers, and it’s going to be an absolutely incredible event, and we’ll have a few surprises. If we’re going to win the midterms, we have to do things differently.”

Gruters said “it was President Trump’s idea, and while most conventions take years to prepare, we’ve turned this vision into a reality in just the last 60 days.”

The event, however, is a gamble — with some Republican consultants close to the administration telling The Post that the event could harm vulnerable candidates by making the Nov. 3 election all about Trump at a time when polls show him with low approval ratings.

It could also become embarrassment if the NFL’s opening nights — on Wednesday and Thursday — claim more viewers than the commander-in-chief.

“I’m all in on Republicans winning. But midterms are referendums on the president, and having the same Republicans talk even more about the administration isn’t increasing our numbers,” one GOP consultant said.

A second operative close to the White House said “the whole thing is dumb, especially to do [it] on the two opening nights [of the NFL season].”

On Wednesday night, Trump will compete for the nation’s attention while the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks clash in a Super Bowl rematch in a game that airs on NBC. The following night, the convention goes up against the San Francisco 49ers-Los Angeles Rams matchup on Netflix.

‘Haters will be pleasantly surprised’

Trump is expected to rattle off a variety of feats that he often claims should deliver Republicans a mandate for the remainder of his term — including strong-arming pharmaceutical companies into lowering prices and pushing through Congress new tax breaks on tips, overtime and Social Security payments.

“Haters will be pleasantly surprised by the amount of policy focus in the speeches,” said a person involved in planning the event.

“They will mention the president and the Republican Congress’ victories — policy wins and tax cuts.”

Incumbent presidents almost always lose House seats in the midterms, with George W. Bush the most recent to buck the trend in 2002 as he avenged the 9/11 attacks a year prior.

The GOP currently holds a tenuous five-seat edge — and the party lost 41 House seats in 2018 during Trump’s first term.

Trump, aware of the historical context, devised the convention — Democrats are not hosting their own midterm convention — as a way to upend the expected outcome.

Although a redistricting war gave Republicans an edge in a handful of districts, economic concerns in particular have dragged on the party in power — with the Iran War causing an uptick in inflation and gas prices.

The prime time slots after 8 p.m. eastern time go to a mix of well-known and up-and-coming figures.

On Wednesday, the coveted window includes Medicare and Medicaid chief Dr. Mehmet Oz, Florida gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds, Arizona House candidate Jay Feely, Michigan House candidate Mike Bouchard and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

The Thursday primetime slot includes Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Dallas Mayor Eric Johnson, former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr.

“Everybody wants to be there, but we’re really asking only those Candidates that are in tight Races, a little up, a little down, or even, to speak,” the president wrote on Truth Social Tuesday.

“We want to save the ‘stage’ for them. We don’t need people who are up 45 points, and have been in office for 30 years, as much as we love them all!”

Candidates in tight races have chosen different approaches to the convention, which is shorter than a standard presidential-year summit.

Perennially vulnerable Maine Sen. Susan Collins and South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds, whose Democrat-backed independent challenger claims to have pulled even in internal polling, are skipping the convention altogether. 

Both Collins and Rounds have distanced themselves from Trump’s weeks-old trade war with Canada, noting the likely effect of retaliatory tariffs on their states’ exports.

But others in competitive races aren’t just showing up — they are appearing on stage.

New York Rep. Mike Lawler, whose district was won by Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024, and Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who faces a tough challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown, are among the speakers.

So too is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is neck-and-neck with Democrat James Talarico in the state’s hotly contested Senate race. Paxton, who has faced a litany of scandals, could benefit from Trump’s embrace in the heavily Republican state.
news.summary: The two-day gathering — nicknamed “Trump-a-Palooza” — offers free publicity for Republicans as they attempt to brand Democrats as "socialists" and features a slew of fundraising events to help the party grow its already large cash advantage to beat back bleak polls pointing to a possible November wipeout.

news.title: Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Democratic Senate primary
news.text:
Rep. Chris Pappas won New Hampshire’s Democratic Senate primary on Tuesday, advancing to the November general election in a race that could help determine control of the Senate.

Pappas defeated progressive medical scientist Karishma Manzur, his most prominent opponent, along with David Jarvis, Maxwell Saal and John Vail, to claim the Democratic nomination for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.

“Today, the voters of New Hampshire have sent a clear message: they're fed up with what's happening in our politics, and they're ready for change,” Pappas told his supporters in Manchester, New Hampshire.

Manzur, a democratic socialist who has never held elected office, sought to capitalize on frustration with the Democratic establishment and argued that the party needed a more progressive voice in Washington.

Pappas’ victory is a win for Democrats who believe a pragmatic candidate with a record of winning competitive elections gives the party its strongest chance of holding the seat in November. New Hampshire is expected to be competitive and critical territory for both parties’ efforts to control the chamber.

Pappas will face former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu, the brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu and son of former Gov. John H. Sununu, in a key race for Senate control.

The New Hampshire Democrat sought to tie his Republican rival to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu, arguing that voters deserve a senator focused on the state.“We got to turn the page on Donald Trump's reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy, and on costs--and this is not the time to turn it back to a failed politician from the past,” Pappas said. "It is time to look ahead to the future, and that's what we're fighting for in this campaign."

Sununu, during his victory speech Tuesday night, cast Pappas as an “ineffective, partisan and out of touch” career politician. He also challenged Pappas to 10 debates — one in each New Hampshire county — as the two move into the general election campaign.

A four-term congressman representing New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, Pappas has repeatedly won in the politically competitive Granite State. Before entering Congress in 2019, he served three terms on the state Executive Council and previously served in the New Hampshire House. A Manchester native and former co-owner of his family’s restaurant, the Puritan Backroom, Pappas became the first openly gay person to represent New Hampshire in Congress.

On the campaign trail, Pappas emphasized pocketbook concerns, arguing that Democrats need to focus on the cost of housing, healthcare and other everyday expenses. He also promoted proposals to lower taxes for working families and small businesses, reduce prescription drug costs and rein in corporate influence in Washington. Pappas made government ethics a central theme of his campaign, including pushing to ban members of Congress from trading stocks and reduce the role of big money in politics.

Pappas raised more than $15.3 million, according to Federal Election Commission data, compared with about $415,000 for Manzur — a nearly $15 million fundraising gap.

Pappas secured key endorsements from former President Barack Obama, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Vice President Kamala Harris and New Hampshire Sens. Shaheen and Maggie Hassan.

Manzur, meanwhile, drew support from progressive figures and groups, including former Rep. Jamaal Bowman, former Ohio state Sen. Nina Turner, Progressive Democrats of America and the climate group 350NH Action.

The primary also offered a test of the Democratic Party’s direction. Manzur presented voters with a more aggressively progressive alternative, while Pappas argued that New Hampshire voters were looking for an independent-minded Democrat focused on affordability and results rather than ideological labels.

For Pappas, the task now shifts from winning over Democratic voters to holding together a broader coalition in a state where statewide elections are often decided by narrow margins — and where the outcome could reverberate far beyond New Hampshire.
news.author: Susan Del Percio

news.title: Anthony DiLorenzo Wins Primary in Boost to Donald Trump
news.text: President Donald Trump was dealt a victory after his endorsed candidate Anthony DiLorenzo won the Republican primary in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District on Tuesday. DiLorenzo defeated Hollie Noveletsky, who served as the former vice chair of the New Hampshire Republican Party. He received 51.5 percent of the vote to Noveletsky’s 26.8 percent, according to The Associated Press, which called the race at 8 p.m. ET on Tuesday. Trump’s endorsement has remained powerful in recent Republican primaries, but his support doesn't necessarily guarantee a candidate will win. In some recent primaries, other Republicans defeated Trump-backed candidates. DiLorenzo’s victory is the latest sign of Trump’s ongoing popularity among GOP voters. It comes after a recent poll from the University of New Hampshire gave a warning sign about DiLorenzo’s chances, showing Noveletsky with a 3-point lead, 28 percent to 25 percent. It had surveyed 443 Republican voters from August 20 to 24, 2026. Donald Trump’s Endorsement Record Trump endorsed DiLorenzo, a local businessman, on Truth Social on July 13, praising him as a “very successful Businessman and Entrepreneur.” “It is my Great Honor to endorse America First Patriot, Anthony DiLorenzo, who is running to represent the fantastic people of New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District!” he wrote at the time. Trump has endorsed hundreds of candidates across the country ahead of the midterms, with Ballotpedia giving him a 96 percent success rate in primaries this year. Some of his endorsed candidates have lost to other Republicans. In Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District, for instance, Representative Andy Ogles, backed by Trump, lost to Charlie Hatcher, the state’s former commissioner of agriculture who was endorsed by Governor Bill Lee. In Florida’s 19th District, Trump-backed Catalina Lauf also lost her primary to Jim Schwartzel in the race to succeed Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor. Trump’s preferred candidate in Michigan’s 8th District, Amir Hassan, also lost his primary to rival Thomas J. Smith, a Republican who suspended his campaign and endorsed another candidate prior to the election. Several Trump-backed gubernatorial candidates have lost their primaries, including Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones in Georgia, Representative Randy Feenstra in Iowa, Mike Lindell in Minnesota, Lieutenant Governor Pamela Evette in South Carolina and Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming. Trump’s endorsement record has been bolstered by his enduring popularity among the Republican primary electorate. His national approval rating has plummeted since his return to the Oval Office, but Republicans continue to support his administration, according to recent polls. The latest poll from YouGov and The Economist showed that Trump’s overall net approval stood at -24 points, 36 percent approving and 60 percent disapproving. Among Republicans, his net approval rating was +62 points, 80 percent approving and 18 percent disapproving. The survey included 1,592 adults and ran from August 28 to 31, 2026. Republicans’ Chances of Flipping NH-01 Polling on the district has not been made public, but prediction markets favor Democrats to hold the seat, which is currently held by Democratic Representative Chris Pappas, who is running for Senate in the Granite State. As of Tuesday, Kalshi gave Democrats an 88 percent chance of victory, while Polymarket placed Democrats’ chances at 89 percent. The district backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by over 2 points in the 2024 election, so it is competitive on paper. But Democrats believe the national environment, driven by Trump’s declining national approval rating, should keep the seat in their hands in November. Republicans, however, are hoping that the so-called blue wave won’t sweep New Hampshire, as polls show GOP Governor Kelly Ayotte favored to win reelection, and an increasingly competitive Senate race. New Hampshire’s 1st District is generally the more competitive of the two districts and comprises the eastern parts of the state. Democrats typically win large margins in places like Portsmouth and Dover. It also includes Manchester, which leans Democratic but not overwhelmingly; Harris won the city by fewer than 8 points. Democrats also do well in the tourist areas near the White Mountains. Republicans, however, do better in suburban areas outside Manchester in southern New Hampshire, as well as in towns in the Lakes Region, keeping the seat competitive in recent elections. Pappas had won reelection by wider margins in recent cycles, winning by 8 points in 2024. He also defeated Karoline Leavitt, who would go on to become White House press secretary, by about 8 points in 2022. He has represented the swing district since 2019. Forecasters give Democrats an advantage. The Cook Political Report considers the race Likely Democrat, while Sabato’s Crystal Ball rates it Leans Democratic. news.summary: A New Hampshire congressional primary was the latest test of Trump's endorsement power.

news.title: Sununu, Pappas to Go Head-to-Head in New Hampshire Senate Race
news.text:
CONCORD, N.H.—New Hampshire voters have sent former Republican U.S. Sen. John Sununu and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas to battle it out for the open New Hampshire Senate seat in November.

Voters chose from a crowded field of contestants for a seat that both parties consider key to their plans to control the upper chamber of Congress.

On the Republican ballot, Sununu and former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, along with six other candidates, vied for the nomination.

Sununu won a New Hampshire Senate seat in 2002, defeating then-Gov. Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Shaheen defeated Sununu in their 2008 rematch.

Brown, meanwhile, was elected in Massachusetts in 2010 to serve out the three remaining years of the late Democratic U.S. Sen. Edward Kennedy’s final term.

However, he was defeated in 2012 and so never took on a full term. Brown moved to New Hampshire and challenged Shaheen in 2014, losing only narrowly.

Brown endorsed President Donald Trump during his 2016 campaign, and the president later appointed him ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during his first term.

In this primary election, however, Trump backed Sununu. This is despite Sununu’s endorsement of Trump rival Nikki Haley in the 2024 election.

Sununu’s campaign outraised Brown’s, taking in $4.1 million to Brown’s $2.2 million.

On the Democratic side, Pappas was seen as the front-runner and gathered support from many high-profile Democrats, including Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), former Gov. John Lynch, and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The lawmaker has served in the House since 2019 but has held public office consistently since graduating from college in 2002.

Pappas defeated Republican Karoline Leavitt, then-Trump White House press aide who later became White House press secretary, in New Hampshire’s First Congressional District in the 2022 election.

Self-proclaimed Independent progressive voter Timothy Willis held signs encouraging voters to “vote [for] progressives” outside a polling location. He told The Epoch Times that he supports Democrat Karishma Manzur for Senate.

Willis said he has voted for Pappas in the past, but more information has come to light about Pappas and his support from PACs, or political action committees, and what Willis sees as a disconnect from voters.

“When they had a debate at Channel Nine in New Hampshire the other night, and Karishma got out and greeted her supporters. Chris Pappas just ignored his supporters and went right in. He just does not seem too genuine.”

Willis said he isn’t at all sure Manzur would win in November, but he thinks it’s important to be proactive. The activist said he doesn’t subscribe to the notion that voters should “just hold your nose and vote for the lesser of two evils.”

“We have to fight. We have to be more proactive, and we just need to get it done.”

Merrimack County Attorney candidate Meg Hagaman, a Republican, stood with Democratic New Hampshire House candidate Tracy Bricchi and told The Epoch Times that they’re voting for Sununu and Pappas, respectively.

Bricchi said she is voting for Pappas because she believes “he has the best interests of New Hampshire people in mind,” and that his political history shows a person who has “done his best given the climate that he’s worked in.”

When asked if she thinks Pappas can win in November, she took a lengthy pause before saying hesitantly, “I have to say yes.”

Hagaman, however, said she supports Sununu due to his “sensible leadership skills.”

“We know he’s already had experience in the Senate,” Hagaman told The Epoch Times. “He’s had a lot of experience governing, and I think he is someone who wants to put New Hampshire’s people first. And I think he will go to Washington with a lot of sensible thoughts.”

Four other candidates also hoped to take the Democratic nomination, including Manzur, a progressive activist and democratic socialist.

Polling from the University of New Hampshire shows that Pappas still held the lead as of late August.

Shaheen, 79, announced in March 2025 that she wouldn’t seek reelection. She was the first woman to serve as both governor and senator in the United States.

Also on the ballot are nominees for governor, the U.S. House of Representatives, and other state offices.

In addition to the New Hampshire seat, Republicans are targeting the two Senate seats held by Democrats Gary Peters of Michigan and Tina Smith of Minnesota, who are also retiring.
news.author: Savannah Hulsey Pointer

news.title: GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington to face off for New Hampshire governorship
news.text: New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, will face off against Democrat Cinde Warmington in November’s general election, NBC News projects, as she seeks another two-year term. Ayotte did not face any major challenges in the GOP primary; Warmington ran unopposed in the Democratic primary. New Hampshire is one of two states — Vermont is the other — where Republican governors are up for re-election after then-Vice President Kamala Harris won the state in 2024. Ayotte, a former state attorney general and U.S. senator, was out of politics for several years between her loss for re-election in 2016 and her successful campaign for governor in 2024. Warmington served on New Hampshire’s Executive Council, which helps oversee the state budget, from 2021 to 2025. She ran for governor in 2024 and lost in the primary. She has also worked as a healthcare attorney and in healthcare management. Warmington is, like many Democrats, focusing her campaign on affordability, while Ayotte is touting accomplishments of her first two years in office. Ayotte is leading in the early polls and has raised more money, and The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, a nonpartisan election analysis website, rates the race as “leans Republican.”
news.summary: Warmington was unopposed in the Democratic primary, while Ayotte faced nominal opposition before she won her primary, NBC News projects.
news.author: Lauren Zola

news.title: LIVE PRIMARY RESULTS: Will DSA Score Again in New Hampshire?
news.text:
Welcome back to another test of the Democrat sanity system! And, perhaps, the national sanity broadcast system as well. Voters go to the polls today in New Hampshire to nominate candidates from both parties for the Senate, the House, and for governor. 

In the Senate primaries, though, we should make it three parties. Incumbent Democrat Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement last year, and House Democrat Chris Pappas jumped into the race immediately. Pappas looked to be a cinch for the nomination. However, Democratic Socialist Karishma Manzur entered the race late – and may have picked up some momentum. The most recent poll from the University of New Hampshire only has Pappas ahead by 47/34, hardly a confidence-builder for the Democrat establishment. Our election night partners at Decision Desk HQ try to follow the money, but also note that the GOP seems to be playing catch-up in a potential November flip:

But money talks, so it may be a tell that two pro-Pappas groups felt the need to fork out $175,000 in the closing days for get-out-the-vote calls and texts supporting the congressman. Defend the Vote made a $100,000 outlay, while pro-LGBTQ Equality PAC spent $75,000 (if elected, Pappas would become the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate).The purple-tinted Granite State has had a light-blue lean in recent federal elections, last voting for a Republican for Senate in 2010 and a GOP presidential contender in 2000. But that recent UNH poll also found Pappas narrowly trailing GOP frontrunner, ex-Sen. John E. Sununu, 45%-43%. To be clear, this was Sununu’s best recent poll result, and the Decision Desk HQ forecast gives Democrats about a 4 in 5 shot of winning the seat. Still, Democrats are more concerned about holding this seat.The Sununu name is part of the path to a plausible Republican victory in what otherwise looks like a Democratic-leaning year. A former U.S. senator and representative, Sununu won this very Senate seat in 2002 versus Shaheen before losing a rematch against her in the blue-wave year of 2008. Despite that defeat, Sununu remains a prestigious brand name in New Hampshire politics. In January 2025, John’s popular young brother Chris finished off an eight-year run as governor before deciding against his own bid for Senate. Their father, John H. Sununu, served as New Hampshire’s governor for three two-year terms in the 1980s and then as President George H.W. Bush’s first chief of staff.

In other words, the GOP has an uphill battle in the Granite State no matter what. However, having Sununu ready to return puts them in as good a position as Republicans can manage. That may be even more true, given Sununu's nearly 20-year absence, which may allow him to present a more independent positioning in the general election. If Democrats nominate Manzur, Sununu's odds may improve considerably. 

The only other major drama will be for Pappas' House seat in NH-01, a D+2 district that narrowly went to Kamala Harris in 2024. Shaheen's daughter Stefany is running against former Marine Corps vet Maura Sullivan, and they have both been raising significant amounts of money, combining for about $6 million already. Outside spending has been almost twice that number. Whoever wins will likely face off against Trump-endorsed, self-funding entrepreneur Anthony DiLorenzo, although fellow entrepreneur Hollie Noveletsky still has a shot.

Most polls close in New Hampshire at 7 PM ET, although a few will remain open until 8 PM ET. Follow the results tonight with our partners at Decision Desk HQ, and get the most reliable calls in the business!

news.title: Ousted '60 Minutes' journalist breaks silence on MAGA mouthpiece 'dilettantes' at CBS
news.text:
A veteran "60 Minutes" journalist fired in May said unqualified online personalities have taken over CBS News, and that he was pushed out for refusing White House talking points.

Guy Campanile, who was managing editor of "60 Minutes" until his dismissal in May, made the accusations in a statement he posted to his Facebook page.

Media reporter Justin Baragona published the full text on X on Tuesday, five days before the newsmagazine begins its 59th season under new management.

Campanile said he had stayed quiet for months because it is wise to remain silent when emotions are raw, and that after reflection he was prepared to describe what he experienced during his final year at the program, according to the statement.

In the statement, Campanile named six colleagues who lost their jobs alongside him, including correspondent Scott Pelley and executive producer Tanya Simon.

"Tanya Simon, Draggan Mihailovich, Matthew Polevoy, Scott Pelley, Sharyn Alfonsi, Cecilia Vega and I refused to be accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television," Campanile wrote.

Campanile described the specific editorial demands he says the group resisted, including instructions about which sources to interview.

"We would not compromise our principles or reputations by jamming unverifiable notions or White House talking points into our reporting. We objected when told to conduct interviews arranged by the administration," he wrote.

"To be clear - we were told to leave because we insisted on doing our jobs," Campanile added.

Campanile wrote that the firings were part of a wider collapse he traced to commercial and political pressure on newsrooms rather than to any single decision at his former program.

"What has happened recently at 60 Minutes – where I believe editorial independence has become a casualty of corporate priorities and ideological intrusion – was tragic," he wrote.

Campanile reserved his sharpest language for the people he says are now making programming decisions at major news organizations, according to the statement.

"Making matters worse is the cadre of self-described influencers and online opinionists who market themselves as 'journalists'. Some have been given control of our most precious reporting institutions — including CBS News," he wrote.

"Many of these newsroom managers have never been exposed to the depths of poverty, the ravages of war or the heartbreak of disaster. Yet these dilettantes and their enablers make critical programming decisions based on what might trend online over the next few hours," Campanile continued.

Campanile wrote that he spent two-thirds of his life at CBS and left the company's West 57th Street offices with his head held high and his integrity intact.

"I cannot remain silent as trust built over decades by my colleagues and mentors is wrecked. The audience deserves so much better," he wrote.

Campanile closed by quoting Thomas Jefferson on press freedom, saying it is dangerous to ignore the warning, and then addressed the colleagues he left behind.

"Hold the line. Don't give an inch because they will keep scraping away until there's nothing left worth a damn," he wrote.

The firings Campanile describes took place on the last Thursday of May and became known inside the company as Black Thursday, according to New York magazine, which reported the day in detail last month.

Simon had led the program for a year and was called into an early meeting with CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss and CBS News president Tom Cibrowski, where she was fired instead of reviewing the season as she expected, the magazine reported. Her deputy Draggan Mihailovich, producers Campanile and Matthew Polevoy, and correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were dismissed the same day.

Campanile learned of his own dismissal on a Zoom call as he was scheduled to leave for the airport to report a story with correspondent Lesley Stahl in Spain, according to the magazine. Charles Forelle, one of Weiss's deputies, told him he could still shoot the segment even though he was no longer on the program, and Campanile declined.

Pelley was fired the next day after telling an all-staff meeting that Weiss was "murdering 60 Minutes," the magazine reported.

Weiss had arrived at CBS News in October 2025, hired by Paramount owner David Ellison into the newly created position of editor-in-chief, according to New York magazine.

In December, Weiss pulled a story by Alfonsi on the deportation of Venezuelan migrants to a Salvadoran prison and asked producers to add an interview with White House adviser Stephen Miller or another Trump official, the magazine reported. Alfonsi wrote to colleagues that Weiss "spiked" the story "for political optics," and the piece eventually aired on Jan. 18 with no significant changes.

Pelley later alleged that Weiss urged him to inject "falsehoods and bias" into a segment on the killings of two protesters by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis, according to the magazine. Vega said executives asked her to add footage showing protesters attacking people who had been incorrectly identified as agents of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and that she found "no credible examples" of such behavior.

CBS News disputed both accounts, the magazine reported, and people who defend Weiss have said her conflict with the staff was about management rather than politics.

Weiss also involved herself in booking guests, an unusual role for a senior network executive, according to New York magazine. She personally arranged interviews with Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, and traveled to Mar-a-Lago to observe Norah O'Donnell's interview with President Donald Trump.

In March, Weiss booked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and assigned the interview to chief Washington correspondent Major Garrett, who was not on the program's roster, the magazine reported. She did the same with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May, even though Stahl had spent months pursuing that interview.

The pressure on the program began before Weiss arrived. Paramount agreed in July 2025 to pay $16 million to settle a lawsuit Trump filed over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, according to CBS News. The money went to Trump's future presidential library; the agreement included no apology, and the program agreed to release transcripts of future interviews with presidential candidates.

Campanile raised the settlement with Weiss during her first two weeks on the job, asking for her view, and she declined to answer, saying her response could leak, according to New York magazine. A former staffer told the magazine that she failed the test from the start.

The corporate stakes have grown since. Trump told reporters in December that CNN should be sold as part of any deal for its parent company, saying the people who have run the network are "a disgrace", the Washington Post reported.

In April, David Ellison hosted a dinner in Washington honoring Trump and the First Amendment, attended by CBS News executives and journalists, including Weiss, according to Variety.

A Paramount shareholder sued the Ellisons this summer, alleging they cut an illegal deal with Trump to win government approval of their bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, Variety reported. The suit claims they offered the president a chance to improperly funnel cash to him by settling his legal claims against CNN, and promised that CNN anchors he dislikes would be fired after a takeover.

"This lawsuit recycles allegations that have already been reported and already addressed," a Paramount spokesperson said in a statement to Variety, adding that "no commitments from either David or Larry Ellison have been made to any government body, State AG, or federal agency regarding the future of CNN or any other news property, other than the goal to deliver truth-based journalism."

"Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve — not to any party or cause," David Ellison wrote in a New York Times opinion piece quoted by Variety, in which he said the real question being litigated is whether he can be trusted as a steward of CNN.

The Department of Justice signed off on the $111 billion merger in June without requiring Paramount to sell any assets or accept any conditions, CNN reported.

The merger has not closed. A 12-state antitrust lawsuit led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, is holding up the deal and is set for trial in March 2027 unless the two sides settle, Variety reported. Ellison has threatened to move Paramount out of California if the transaction is not completed by Oct. 1, when the company begins owing Warner Bros. investors $7 million a day.

The new season begins Sunday with a segment by O'Donnell featuring interviews with Hegseth, Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, and Adm. Brad Cooper, the operational commander of the war with Iran, according to Deadline.
